column2: The last edition of the Civil Service List was submitted to parliament at the first session of 1919 and contained the records up to the 1st April, 1918. The provision which required the Civil Service Commission to issue the annual Civil Service List was deleted from the Civil Service Act of 1918. Consequently since that date there has been no statutory provision for the publication of an annual list.

column1: The work of reclassification which has been in progress since the fall of 1918 has made it difficult if not impossible to compile a Civil Service List which could have been even approximately accurate by the time it was ready for distribution. The commission has not therefore considered it advisable to submit any recommendation to the government in this matter up to the present time.

column2: Owing to the entire permanent service being now under the Civil Service Commission a complete list to-day would contain at least three times as many names as the 1918 edition and would be correspondingly expensive to produce. The commission would not be prepared to proceed with its preparation save under direct instructions from the government.
Answered by No. 1.

666039,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.38.2,1923-05-28,6cab8398-dae1-4e94-b6be-0177cdcd9b99,ca.m.8626,Sir HENRY DRAYTON:,,CANADA SHIPPING ACT-PILOTAGE,,,"Will the minister explain this bill?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Henry Lumley Drayton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6cab8398-dae1-4e94-b6be-0177cdcd9b99&Language=E&Section=ALL
666040,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.38.3,1923-05-28,4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c,ca.m.491,Mr. LAPOINTE:,Minister of Marine and Fisheries,CANADA SHIPPING ACT-PILOTAGE,,,I explained the proposed legislation fully when the resolution was before the committee and my hon. friend was present; I can only repeat what I then said. The law as it is does not allow any discretion to the pilotage authority, in ports other than Quebec, Montreal, Halifax, and St. John, to refuse a certificate to the master or the mate of a vessel who may apply for it. The object of the bill is to replace the word ""shall"" by the word ""may"" and add the words ""if his application be approved by the pilotage authority."" At present the pilot-

age authorities, after the ordinary examinations and upon payment of the dues, are compelled to deliver a certificate to the master or mate making the application. The necessity for the change has been forcibly brought to the attention of the department through a special case which arose this season in the pilotage district of Miramichi. The channel there is very narrow, and capable men have to be employed as pilots. We cannot expect pilots to spend all their time there if their services are not always required; under these conditions they have no option but to seek other means of livelihood, thus leaving the port without competent pilots. The bill is necessitated by an opinion of the Department of Justice that under the law as it stands the pilotage authorities have to grant the certificate. Under the amendment the master or mate is allowed to pass an examination, and be granted the certificate only when the pilotage authorities approve.

,Liberal,,Ernest Lapointe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c&Language=E&Section=ALL

From my own experience in business it seems to me it would be a very good idea if the agents of companies, or the companies themselves, were compelled to deliver to the insured a copy of the application at the time it is taken. I have, as a matter of fact, a case pending now, and there are many such cases where these policies are filled in, as a matter of convenience, by the agent of the company. I am not finding fault with that, but apparently the agent sometimes takes certain things for granted and inserts them himself, and then later on they turn out to be incorrect not having been read over at the time by the

666081,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.40.28,1923-05-28,89103d9d-627c-4f56-8113-57b0d3865982,ca.m.3867,Mr. FIELDING:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,INSURANCE ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT",,,"I shall be pleased to leave the bill in committee and discuss the matter suggested by my hon. friend with the Superintendent of Insurance.

,Liberal,,William Stevens Fielding,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=89103d9d-627c-4f56-8113-57b0d3865982&Language=E&Section=ALL
666082,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.40.29,1923-05-28,4f144b8d-0f62-4502-b6eb-6bf2aa0faaad,ca.m.1477,Mr. MANION:,,INSURANCE ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT",,,"May I ask a question' I notice in glancing through the notes of the bill-I confess I have not read it over carefully-that the measure seems entirely for the purpose of protecting the insurance company, and I was wondering if the draftsman- I am not referring to the minister himself but to the official who drew up the bill- in any way took into account the very large number of owners of automobiles in the coun-

try, and if he did not draw the bill wholly with the object of protecting the company. In other words has the matter been gone into sufficiently fully by the draftsman to ensure that the companies are not making the regulations so strict as to vitiate, in certain cases, or do away with, the insurance. I hope that the interests of the owner of the automobile are being looked after. I know that the minister would not ignore that point, but I have seen bills put through the House on some matters in which the effect of all the provisions had not been thoroughly looked into. Now the owners of automobiles in the country would not become thoroughly familiar with a policy of this kind whereas the company would be looking entirely to its own interest. I simply point out that phase of the question to the minister.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Robert James Manion,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4f144b8d-0f62-4502-b6eb-6bf2aa0faaad&Language=E&Section=ALL
666083,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.40.30,1923-05-28,89103d9d-627c-4f56-8113-57b0d3865982,ca.m.3867,Mr. FIELDING:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,INSURANCE ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT",,,"I shall draw my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the Superintendent of Insurance. ,Liberal,,William Stevens Fielding,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=89103d9d-627c-4f56-8113-57b0d3865982&Language=E&Section=ALL
666084,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.40.31,1923-05-28,6cab8398-dae1-4e94-b6be-0177cdcd9b99,ca.m.8626,Sir HENRY DRAYTON:,,INSURANCE ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT",,,"There is just one thing, going rather to the principle of this matter, that I would like to draw to my hon. friend's attention. On glancing over the act now I see that exceptions to insurability are made by the act itself. The usual principle as to insurance is that the insurance, when made^ is an absolute contract unless exceptions are stipulated, and for the purpose of helping the public the law provides that these notices shall be printed very distinctly. In some instances, I think-I am speaking from recollection-red ink or larger type has to be used if the company desires to contract itself outside of the ordinary liability of an insurer. In other words, the exceptions have to be brought to the attention of the insured. Now, I point out to my hon. friend that this bill changes the rule altogether. This bill says that unless otherwise specifically stated in the policy of insurance, the company shall not be liable in a whole list of cases; for example if the interest of the insured in the automobile is not that of sole ownership, and so on. A man might very well desire to insure a partial but real interest which he had in an automobile just as much as if he owned it wholly himself, and I really think it should be pointed

out to him in black and white in his policy that that partial interest is not insurable. Then again, a man may well insure his automobile and have to raise a little money on it; that will not be looked upon as a very heinous thing to do. But under this bill if a man insures his automobile and happens to have or subsequently gives a mortgage, or a lien, against it the policy is void, though there is nothing in the policy to show that such is the case. I would suggest to the minister that he should look into the effect of this bill and see whether we really ought to depart from a pretty well settled principle in connection with insurance, namely, that if the insurer desires to make exceptions to his general liability the exceptions must be clearly shown on the face of the policy.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Henry Lumley Drayton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6cab8398-dae1-4e94-b6be-0177cdcd9b99&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,William Stevens Fielding,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=89103d9d-627c-4f56-8113-57b0d3865982&Language=E&Section=ALL
666086,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.40.33,1923-05-28,91930a35-bc92-459a-b10f-a32cc5d218fe,ca.m.3557,Mr. BOYS:,Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942),INSURANCE ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT",,,"Would the minister allow me to make another suggestion or two which might be considered by the superintendent when he is speaking to him. I would like to suggest that a copy of an application should always be given to the assured. Supposing, as often happens, loss is sustained and some question arises. The solicitor wants to see the application that his client has signed, but he has not got it. There is nothing which compels an insurance company to provide it, and while most of them do some are unwilling. I think there should be a clause in the bill which would compel an insurance company to provide a copy of the application upon the request of the assured or his solicitor. Then I would like this further suggestion to be considered: There should be a clause that the assured or his authorized agent should be permitted at any time to inspect the original application in the possession of the company. My reason for suggesting that is this. As I said before, very often answers are filled in by the agent and you cannot find that out by a typewritten copy. But if the opportunity was afforded of seeing the original application you could tell whose handwriting it is in, and get at what you want that way. I would like such a clause as that to be included if possible.

666092,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.41.1.4,1923-05-28,6cab8398-dae1-4e94-b6be-0177cdcd9b99,ca.m.8626,Sir HENRY DRAYTON:,,OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUGS BILL,SENATE AMENDMENTS,,I take it that those are the first two.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Henry Lumley Drayton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6cab8398-dae1-4e94-b6be-0177cdcd9b99&Language=E&Section=ALL
666093,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.41.1.5,1923-05-28,50634114-351e-4c08-8b61-8698a41f8814,ca.m.1247,Mr. BELAND:,Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health,OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUGS BILL,SENATE AMENDMENTS,,The first two involve only the addition of one word to the interpretation clause. The other amendments are more important but as far as we are concerned we have no objection at all to them. They make the intention of the bill clear. I refer to the amendment to clause 4 of the bill, which is the penalty clause. It has been divided in two, one having reference to indictment and the other to summary conviction, a penalty being provided in each case. The fourth amendment refers to section 14, on which there was some discussion in this House, and it has reference to the onus of proof. The amendment reads:

Where any person is charged with an offence under paragraph (a), (d) or (e) of section 4 of this act, it shall not be necessary for the prosecuting authority to establish that the accused had not a license from the minister, or was not otherwise authorized to commit the act complained of, and if the accused pleads or alleges that he has such license or other authority, the burden of proof thereof shall be upon the person so charged.
It makes it a little milder, and I think more acceptable. The last amendment provides for the insertion of the words ""and for the revocation of licenses"" after the word
purposes.""
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Henry Lumley Drayton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6cab8398-dae1-4e94-b6be-0177cdcd9b99&Language=E&Section=ALL
666097,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.42.3,1923-05-28,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil):,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs,DOMINION LANDS ACT AMENDMENT-COAL,,,I think hon. members of the House will remember that the
Dominion Lands-Coal

present bill was submitted as an amendment to the Cancellation Act introduced by myself, to validate cancellation of leases. At that time I opposed this amendment, pointing out that the leases in question, were placed under the control of the Governor in Council and were not in the hands of the minister for disposal. Since that time, I presume, hon. members will have noticed that this has been the matter of a rather lengthy controversy in the Senate, both as to the question of the leases and as to the question of the issuing of the fiat in connection with those leases. Hon. members will remember that the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) introduced legislation on Friday evening for the purpose of the withdrawal of the fiat, and again the Senate has passed this amendment, and I am prepared to accept it, and will ask the House to accept it. It will place these lands under the control of parliament rather than under the control of the minister or the government.

,Liberal,,Charles A. Stewart,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b&Language=E&Section=ALL
666098,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.42.4,1923-05-28,6cab8398-dae1-4e94-b6be-0177cdcd9b99,ca.m.8626,Sir HENRY DRAYTON:,,DOMINION LANDS ACT AMENDMENT-COAL,,,I did not notice that there had been any great conflict in the Senate. It seemed to me that the government representatives in the Senate realized that a great mistake had been made last year, and that the government members in the Senate promoted this legislation; furthermore, that the government members in the Senate, upon looking into the question of the fiat, came to the conclusion that a very great error had been made in issuing that fiat. A bill has now been brought over from the Senate, which

4 p.m. will enable the government to recede from a position which was entirely antagonistic to the real interests of the people. That is quite clear. I merely rise to point out that I do not think there was a fight in the Senate. I think they recognized unanimously that the present procedure was absolutely right, and I rise to congratulate my hon. friend on doing the right thing now, although he insisted on doing the wrong thing last year.

666114,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.1.1,1923-05-28,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:

That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Dairy Industry Act, 1914, and to provide regulations regarding butter substitute and the re-manufacture of butter, the character and weight of butter, the keeping of records by manufacturers or dealers in
Dairy Industry Act

butter and cheese, and the examination of such records by inspectors, methods of establishing the guilt of persons charged with violation of the Act, and the procedure to be followed in all such cases.
Motion agreed to and House went into committee, Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure) in the chair.",,,,

666115,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.2,1923-05-28,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,"THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"This resolution precedes a bill, which, I think, has not yet been distributed. The purpose of the bill is to amend the Dairy Industry Act, such amendments are being made as time and the changed conditions of the industry have proved to be necessary. Certain changes are provided for in the interpretation clauses with respect to the terms ""inspector"" and ""analyst."" The terms ""milk"" and ""butter fat"" have also been defined in the bill. I do not think the term ""substitute for butter"" is to be found in the bill, but I believe it is in the margin; it refers to the percentage of milk or butter fat that must be contained in butter, and the stipulation is made that this shall be 80 per cent and shall conform to the requirements of the Food and Drug Act.

,Liberal,,William Richard Motherwell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f&Language=E&Section=ALL
666116,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.3,1923-05-28,a4a7d1fa-870b-4590-a260-7e2f460d6e83,ca.m.8566,Mr. TOLMIE:,,THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"That does not refer to oleomargarine?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Simon Fraser Tolmie,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a4a7d1fa-870b-4590-a260-7e2f460d6e83&Language=E&Section=ALL
666117,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.4,1923-05-28,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"No; possibly that may come up at a later stage, but I cannot say with any certainty now whether it will or not. The bill also deals with re-manufactured butter. The term ""manufactured"" has hitherto been misunderstood. Sometimes it is used in reference to the original source of the manufactured article, but occasionally butter is re-made or re-churned, and there is a provision with respect to that practice. Possibly the section that is of most interest is that which deals with the weight of butter. In connection with charges that have been made in the past in relation to underweight in butter packages, there has been experienced a great deal of difficulty in proving that there has actually been such underweight. This difficulty has been inevitable under the terms of the act as it stands at present, because it is provided that the weight shall be so much at the time that the prints or the bricks were moulded or cut. When a pound print or brick goes to the retailer and is sold over the counter it is seldom the same weight as it was orginally, so that it is obviously exceedingly difficult to obtain a conviction for the selling of a package that is underweight when you have to prove the weight of the butter at the time it was moulded or cut. This term, ""moulded or cut"" is therefore being eliminated; the weight must be one hundred per cent at the time the butter is offered for sale.

,Liberal,,William Richard Motherwell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Conservative (1867-1942),,William Alves Boys,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=91930a35-bc92-459a-b10f-a32cc5d218fe&Language=E&Section=ALL
666119,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.6,1923-05-28,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"Yes. We shall discuss this point later on. There are difficulties in any case, but thi3 is considered to present the minimum difficulty and is most satisfactory inasmuch as it assures the consumer of full weight. As I have said, it is next to impossible to secure any conviction when you have to prove what the weight of the butter was a month or two previously. There are also some other changes with respect to minor matters: certain books must be kept to conform with the new grading system, and provisions are being made with respect to prosecutions and so forth. But these are matters of detail.

666122,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.9,1923-05-28,a4a7d1fa-870b-4590-a260-7e2f460d6e83,ca.m.8566,Mr. TOLMIE:,,THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"Does ""renovated butter"" mean butter made from renovated cream?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Simon Fraser Tolmie,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a4a7d1fa-870b-4590-a260-7e2f460d6e83&Language=E&Section=ALL
666123,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.10,1923-05-28,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"No; this provision simply prohibits the manufacture of renovated butter by the process which is practised in the United States.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Simon Fraser Tolmie,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a4a7d1fa-870b-4590-a260-7e2f460d6e83&Language=E&Section=ALL
666125,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.12,1923-05-28,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"No, it does not prohibit re-chuming. ,Conservative (1867-1942),,Simon Fraser Tolmie,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a4a7d1fa-870b-4590-a260-7e2f460d6e83&Language=E&Section=ALL
666127,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.14,1923-05-28,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"No; when the bill is under consideration I shall explain that feature of it. The ""manna"" that we have just been speaking about may be termed ""filled butter""; it is

filled with other ingredients. In making filled milk the butter fat is extracted from the whole milk and replaced by foreign fats of a similar nature, such as cocoanut oil and peanut oil. The practice is not very general in Canada, but it is quite common in the United States and is prohibited in some nine or ten states. The standards for milk and butter are fixed by order in council under the Food and Drugs Act. In the bill itself there is rather a technical expression which, I think, with the carrying out of the tests embodied in section 1 of the bill stipulating that there shall be 3-5 of butter fat in milk, will have the same effect as prohibiting filled milk, for the simple reason that with this percentage of butter fat in milk there will be no object in adding any other ingredients. Of course, a lot of tests run a good deal higher than 3-5 per cent, which is somewhat low, but it is quite obvious that while the milk contains this percentage it is not simply whole milk with the butter fat extracted.

666143,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.45.30,1923-05-28,39733e89-5c63-44ea-a981-bc71336702b7,ca.m.2365,Mr. SUTHERLAND:,,THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT",,,"Mr. Chairman, there is no questioning the minister's diligence in providing regulations governing the quality of milk, butter and cheese; these dairy products are surrounded with regulations so strict that it is practically impossible for any adulteration to escape detection. The dairymen are not finding fault with such regulations. But I think there is good cause for complaint on their part that such regulations do not apply to those who add base ingredients to dairy products in order to take advantage of the latters' merits. This is a very common practice in this country to-day and it is so general in the United States that, as the minister has pointed out, a number of state legislatures have provided regulations against such adulteration. Reference has been made to ""manna"", which is, I believe, an endeavour to replace butter fat with a baser ingredient so that the compound may be disposed of at a greater profit. It is surprising how ingenious people are in their attempts to. take advantage of something which has merit.

With regard to oleomargarine, which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), I would point out that there is absolutely no fixed standard for this commodity. The packers have the absolute right and privilege to take dairy products into their packing houses, mix base ingredients with them, and sell the compound at an enhanced profit to themselves. Do the committee think it fair to enact regulations so strict with regard to the production of a food that is absolutely essential to the

health of growing children, and at the same time allow the packing houses to adulterate this commodity and dispose of it to the public as a substitute for butter? I think our regulations have been altogether too lax in this respect, and I am surprised that the minister is not taking steps in this bill to provide against these encroachments. You may surround those who are producing dairy products with all these regulations, but you cannot compel them to continue their production unless they find it profitable to do so. During this parliament and in preceding parliaments, advice has been handed out by agricultural experts, as well as by those who are not agricultural experts, as to what should be done to make agriculture a success. It has been suggested that the farmers, particularly those in the West, should go into the live stock business; many who do not know the conditions in that part of the country have held that this is the only hope of salvation for the farmer. At the same time the manufacture of a commodity such as butter, on which there is the lowest duty that applies to any commodity that comes into this country, is surrounded with regulations so strict that they are becoming a nuisance. And the minister gets up to-day and states that extra safeguards are to be provided respecting the butter-fat content of milk and dairy products, but no provision is being made in regard to the encroachment on this commodity oi butter-substitutes which are left free from such regulations as apply to dairy products. Skilled chemists take advantage of the high quality of butter-fat by so treating it, through the substitution or inclusion of cheaper ingredients, as to enable them to impose it on the public-not to supply a reasonable demand, but solely to make a profit out of a product that is not their own and that has real merit. We collect no tariff whatever on the commodities which are being brought into this country and mixed with our dairy products-or if we do, ninety-nine per cent is refunded. We have heard a good deal during the last few weeks about the standing of the two old-line parties in this country on the tariff. It has been stated that stability has been given to the tariff and that both the old parties are protectionist; yet this is the kind of protection that is meted out to those engaged in agriculture. It is not to the credit of the two old parties that this has been allowed. Is there a country under the sun for which nature has done more than it has for Canada from an agricultural standpoint?- an ideal country, outside of the long winters we have, and even these are beneficial in

666158,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.47.1.4,1923-05-28,3738c10d-d188-441d-ad40-3689553b373a,ca.m.9678,Mr. BLACK (Yukon):,,COPYRIGHT ACT,SENATE AMENDMENTS,,Although the Senate amendment, postponing the date of the coming into force of the act until the first day of January, 1924, may be somewhat of an improvement on the clause which would have brought it into force on the first day of July,

column2: the change might just as well not have been made because there is no possibility of Canada adopting the provisions of the latest Berne Convention by the amended date. A much later date should have been placed in the bill, and in this connection I should like to read a memorandum prepared by counsel on behalf of the authors:

column1: I observe that the Senate fixes the first of January,

1924, as the date on which the act is to come into force. They might just as well have left the date the first of July, because there is no probability that an arrangement can be arrived at with the United States by the first of January next.

As you know, Congress does not . assemble until December, and it has before it matters of so much greater concern that the Cabinet will not deal with such a comparatively unimportant thing as copyright relations with Canada until more pressing affairs are out of the way.

If our act comes into force on the 1st of January without a new treaty with the United States, the result will be that works published in the United States after that date will not be protected in Canada.

After having enjoyed this copyright protection in Canada for thirty years, the United States government will undoubtedly consider it an affront that its citizens have been made copyright outlaws in Canada, and it is not likely that the United States will continue the reciprocal protection to Canadian authors which they now enjoy.

In consequence, Canadian authors will lose protection in a county they are chiefly concerned in, and as United States publications will be without protection in Canada, and with the Canadian market flooded with cheap piratical-^ reproductions, Canadian authors will lose the benefit -of Canadian copyright as well.
These results will certainly follow if the Copyright Act comes into force before a new treaty is negotiated with the United States.

In my opinion the new act should not come into force until the first of July, 1924, unless sooner proclaimed. This will give parliament at the next session an opportunity to consider the situation should difficulties develop with the United States in negotiating a copyright treaty. If the government is in earnest in improving the copyright law, it must make 6ure that all our existing international rights are preserved before changing the law.

I would like to know whether the minister has taken that phase into consideration because if, as pointed out by counsel, these are to be the results, we had better bring the act into force late enough so that we shall be absolutely safe.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,George Black,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3738c10d-d188-441d-ad40-3689553b373a&Language=E&Section=ALL
666159,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.47.1.5,1923-05-28,3c716a03-43b1-401d-820f-7921b10e5565,ca.m.6937,Mr. ROBB:,Minister of Trade and Commerce,COPYRIGHT ACT,SENATE AMENDMENTS,,The government are quite aware that there has been a difference of opinion as between the authors,- the song writers, musical writers and the printing trade regarding copyright, but this measure was considered carefully in the House, sent over to the Senate and considered carefully there, and the judgment of the Senate was that the date of coming into effect of the act should be extended until January 1st, 1924. The government concurred in and are willing to accept that amendment. I cannot agree with my hon. friend that anything would be gained by extending the date still further. It seems to me that it would be in the interest of all those concerned in Canada that the Copyright Act should become law. Now, as I understand the matter, the case of Howat is this: Several years ago a law was passed in the state of Kansas making a strike a crime. That would undermine the very foundation of trades unionism, and of the

right of organized labour to conduct its own affairs. Howat happened at that time to be president of his union, and on account of his position was asked to go ahead and call a strike. He thereby came in conflict with the law of the state of Kansas, and as the trial went forward became in that respect a criminal. Let me call attention to the fact that Howat was exercising his responsibility as the president of the union when he proceeded to call the strike, and had the greater part of the union behind him at that time. Later on there was trouble between different sections of the United Mine Workers in the state of Kansas, and Howat was deposed from his position as president. According to my information he has been carrying on a campaign in different parts of the States and in Canada-the

Now let me consider the grounds upon which Howat was refused admission to Canada. According to the press of that date he was denied admission on the ground that he would become a public charge. No immigrant, passenger or other person unless he is a Canadian citizen, or has Canadian domicile, shall be permitted to enter or land in Canada, or in case of having landed in or entered Canada shall be permitted to remain therein, who belongs to any of the following classes, hereinafter called ""prohibited classes""-
From the sub-sections enumerating the classes in question I quote the following:
(j) Persons who in the opinion of the Board of Inquiry or the officer in charge at $ny port of entry are likely to become a public chargfe;

The Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization informs me that Howat's appeal was dismissed on the ground that he was likely to become a public charge. He was coming, on the invitation of the miners of Nova Scotia, to fill a lecture engagement, and there was no probability that he would be left without funds or become stranded in this country and be a charge on the resources of the Dominion. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization had no hesitation whatever in telling me that this was only a technical ground. The min-

ister informs me that instructions have been issued that any man from another country, including Great Britain, seeking entry to Canada who has a prison record shall be excluded. That means that in this case the real reason for excluding Howat was not that he was liable to become a public charge, but tht he had served a prison sentence on account of his having come into conflict with the laws of the state of Kansas.

666174,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.4.1.1,1923-05-28,,,,stagedirection,,,,Labour Delegates Detained
Britain and Liberty

Because Home Secretary Bridgeman deported certain English-born Irishmen from England to Ireland, a powerful British government is confronted with a crisis. Not only has the Englishman's passion for the liberty of the subject compelled return of the deported men and women; there is actual possibility that those responsible for deportations shall be prosecuted and that the ministry shall be censured in the House.

In what other country could such a thing take place? The men and women were of humble, lowly origin; without political influence; antagonistic to the interests of the Crown; and a generally dangerous nuisance. No matter. Their deportation was viewed as an invasion of the liberty of the subject, as an encroachment upon human rights: and immediately the voice of England rose up in compelling protest.
Of this is the greatness, the genius and the glory of the British race.

I should like to appeal to Britishers in this country that we in Canada maintain the best British traditions in dealing with matters of this character. Fundamentally such a decision as this is an attack upon freedom of speech. Only a few weeks ago the Acting Minister of Immigration rejected at the border James Larkin who was coming here to fill a lecture engagement in the city of Montreal. James Larkin afterwards returned to Great Britain. The question of his entry was taken up on the floor of the British House of Commons, and the Home Secretary took the ground that James Larkin could not be prevented from entering England because he was a British subject. Here again we have the same question arising. British subjects have certain rights the world over; they should have those rights in Canada as well as in other parts of the British dominions. It is only a few weeks since the distinguished French publicist Jean Longuet, a personal friend of Ramsay Macdonald, who has lectured throughout the length and breadth of Great Britain, and in the United States was asked to come to this country to fulfil certain lecture engagements in the cities of Montreal and Toronto. He was stopped at the border, but finally, as a special concession, he was allowed to come across into Canada, to fill two engagements, on condition that he would return immediately to the United States. Again let me say that that procedure, which is being carried out apparently as a set policy by the present administration, is not in keeping with the best British traditions.

It has been said, of course, that this man Howat was coming over here to raise some disturbance, and after his detention for several days, after the May Day celebration, it was pointed out that there had been very strange things said on May Day. As a matter of fact, it has been definitely denied that these extreme statements were ever uttered, either

in the eastern part of the country, in Cape Breton, or in the western part of the country at Calgary. Apparently the speeches on that occasion were manufactured by the press, and not made by the men themselves.

Consider the situation. On a general international holiday, May Day, the workers, who form a very considerable portion of the population of this country, desire to celebrate in their own way. In so doing they are simply carrying out the request of the International Federation of Trade Unions. I have here a manifesto issued by that body in Europe, signed by J. H. Thomas, M.P., who cannot be accused of being one of the most radical of the labour members of the British House of Commons. It urges that all over the world the workers will celebrate their international holiday. Howat attempts to come over here to join in these celebrations and he is stopped. As far as the working class is concerned, I would say, in the first instance, that they regard this as an unwarrantable interference with Labour's own private affairs. I am not here to defend Howat, or any one section of the United Mine Workers of America. But, irrespective of its sectional prejudices, Labour contends that labour organizations ought to be able to bring over to this country whatever speakers they wish to select. One man representing one section of the United Mine Workers of America was allowed to come through and address a meeting; another man was stopped at the border. Is it for this government to decide which of the representatives of the unions will be allowed to come to Canada and address meetings? If it is, then it is time that we understood that very clearly. But I suggest that the government is going to undertake a pretty big programme if it is to decide just exactly what kind of policies are to be permitted to be advocated in Canada. Further, we regard this as discriminatory class legislation. I know of no occasion when an international bankers' conference has been prevented from meeting in this country. It is fairly well known to certain members of the committee on Banking and Commerce at the present time that some of the policies of our bankers in this country are actually outlined by bankers on the other side of the border; but we do not have any general objection raised to that, nor does the Minister of Immigration send any instructions to his officials on the border that bankers across the line are to be forbidden admittance to this country because their policies may not be in harmony with the policies of certain people in Canada. Imperialists from Great Britain can without
Labour Delegates Detained

hindrance tour this country and address Canadian clubs from coast to coast on certain public policies; yet the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) actually tells us that other members of the British House of Commons shall not be allowed to enter Canada for the reason that their policies are not consistent with the policies of those who at present sit on the government benches in this Chamber.

I appeal to the House once more, as I have done before, on behalf of these miners of Nova Scotia. I wish the House could understand a little bit more clearly how those men feel in this matter. They charge that in the past their constituencies have been so gerrymandered that it has been extremely difficult for them to elect representatives to the House of Commons. I am not undertaking to argue the case; I know that this is very freely stated in the eastern part of the country. They charge, further, that there have been unfair election tactics. Again, I refrain from arguing the point; I simply state as a fact that the allegation is freely made among the miners. They say that again and again they have sent deputations to the government asking for the most reasonable things, and these have been denied them. Last year they sent a deputation requesting that a royal commission be appointed to go into the whole question of the production of coal in Cape Breton. That commission was refused. This year they sent another deputation praying that the present government carry out its pledges and provide, for the old people among them, some system of pensions. Again their deputation was sent back empty handed. Under these circumstances, is it very much wonder that these men feel resentful. On their invitation, one of their fellow members comes to talk to them on a holiday, and they find that even the fundamental rights of British subjects are denied them, that they are not allowed to discuss these questions, and their guests are turned, back?

I submit that if in reality we are seeking to avoid very serious industrial unrest in this country, if we are really sincere in the desire to bring about reconstruction through constitutional means, then this is the time when we ought to act in the proper spirit. There is no use talking to these men and advising them to use parliamentary methods, while again and again you make it impossible for them so to act. Then when on top of all that they find that they cannot enjoy the fundamental British rights of freedom of discussion, of organization, and so forth, I do not much wonder that there is the very deepest resent-

ment, which sooner or later will manifest itself in ways that may cause apprehension throughout the country. Finally, I would appeal to a government that calls itself Liberal, that the old principles of Liberalism be not trampled under foot. I have no doubt the Acting Minister of Immigration himself thinks that he is acting in the best interests of the country. He says he does not want to stir up trouble; he wants to safeguard the miners from these dangerous demagogues from the United States. I have no doubt he is sincere; but I believe he is mistaken in his policy. I would again submit that he has gone altogether beyond both the letter and the spirit of the law which he is supposed to administer.",,,,

That is not at all the ground on which he was refused admittance. His partner came into the country because there was no similar reason for refusing to admit him; and he made his speech. But I have to be guided by the circumstances as I find them, in the case of Larkin, in the case of Howat, and in the case of a prisoner who comes to my mind at the moment, who is in a gaol in Montana. I have had half-a-dozen cases of this character since I became minister. I am perfectly willing to go into the merits of each case, but in a general way where people have served prison sentences I take it that it is not the business of the immigration officers

to make an investigation as to why such sentences were imposed, and I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to change that regulation in any particular. If later on it is proven that these men are entitled to come into the country, I have the privilege of admitting them.

666193,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.5.10,1923-05-28,090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056,ca.m.2263,Mr. NEILL:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MARINE AND FISHERIES,,I wish under this heading to make some remarks to the House in connection with the wreck of the Alaskan which took place on the British Columbia coast last winter, and also in connection with the investigation into that wreck. I also wish to hang on to that so to speak, under circumstances which I will narrate, a plea for some further measure of protection in the way of life-saving on the coast of British Columbia. It will take some time for me to outline the case thoroughly, but I will be as brief as possible, and perhaps the fact that I did not waste the time of the House in discussing the budget may incline the committee to be indulgent on this occasion.

I am taking the wreck of the Alaskan as a typical case, although this is one of four wrecks that occurred last winter on this coast within a very limited area. There was loss of life in connection with some of the other wrecks, but there was a total loss of life in
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

the case of the Alaskan. This coast line along which all these wrecks occur lies entirely within my district. It is called the ' Graveyard of the Pacific,"" and it is not a mere euphonious expression for magazine articles; it has behind it a very dread reality I remember the first occasion when I walked along this coast. Every mile or two, sometimes every quarter of a mile, I would come on the remains of a wreck. If it was a sandy stretch the wreck was still there and I have a distinct recollection of a 200-ton boat lying battered among trees on the edge of the sandy beach and far above ordinary high water. The rocky points had also taken toll; every place had a name, such as Michigan point and so on, all due to the fact that boats had gone ashore at these points within the memory of men then living, and in every case with loss of life, in many cases with a total loss of life.

The Alaskan was lost on the 2nd January of this year. The boat belonged to a little company of men living in Victoria or Vancouver. She was bought in the preceding November. Her owners ran her on one trip from Victoria to Barkley sound, which is on the west coast of Vancouver island. On the second trip she was lost with all hands. This boat was built thirty-seven years ago in the United States. I may say that even now-at that time still more so-the standards of shipbuilding in the United States are much less exacting than our Canadian standards. Consequently hon. members can judge of the character of a boat built thirty-seven years ago in the United States. It was constructed either of Douglas fir, known to be a soft wood, or else of Oregon pine, a still softer wood. I am qupting now, with one small exception, entirely from the evidence taken at the investigation'. I have also used the coroner's inquest held on one of the bodies that came ashore and my personal knowledge of the local geography. This investigation was held under government auspices a few months ago. The Alaskan was a steamer of 13 horse power, and had what is known as a water-tube boiler. Her tonnage was not ISO tons but a few hundred pounds under. They build them like that in order to escape the regulation, because any boat of 150 tons or over has to be inspected annually by the government inspectors as regards her hull. Her machinery must be inspected anyhow. So the hull of this thirty-seven year old boat which was going out into the open Pacific in winter time had never been inspected by any government inspector from the time she was
launched. She was bought at the time I am alluding to for 86,000. She was insured for S9,000 forthwith.

On account of the total loss of life I advised the government to have an investigation into the wreck, and this was ordered. Hon. members will recall that I have from time to time asked the government when the report was coming down. The answer given me first was that the report was delayed by the sickness of the stenographer who had taken the evidence, and later on by the sickness of the commissioner. I am not a bit surprised that they were sick. I have read the evidence and the report and their perusal and a comparison of them filled me with nausea. Therefore, I repeat, I am not surprised that anyone would feel inclined to be sick who had any responsibility whatever in the preparation of the report. For the result was a gigantic whitewash. It whitewashed everybody connected with the wreck. The only person not whitewashed was the Almighty, on whom blame was put for sending the storm, although it was a comparatively minor storm because the meteorological report says the morning of the day on which the Alaskan was lost there was only a fresh gale blowing and at night it was nothing more than a strong gale. In their desire to whitewash everybody in sight they even whitewashed a government official who was discharged by the department for neglect of duty in connection with the wreck. He too was covered with this universal coat of whitewash. But while very abundant it was from its very nature extremely thin, and certain very salient and prominent facts stick out which I purpose to bring to the notice of the House.

In the first place I am putting some responsibility on the government-though not by way of blaming the present government or the last government, or even, necessarily, a department; it is probably a condition of affairs that has grown Up; the conditions have changed and the regulations have not. I am not blaming anyone in connection with the government, but the government of the day, as regards the future at least, have a certain responsibility.

Now, it arose in this way: The government appointed, I do not know how many years ago, a wreck commissioner to deal with these investigations of wrecks on the Pacific coast. It is an extremely important work, because the decisions sometimes involve hundreds of thousands of dollars in connection with wrecks or collisions. Well, they allotted to this
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

official $1,500 or $1,600, a year I am not sure which, and in case this might not be enough for a really competent man, whose duties would be very little inferior to those of a judge, they said: ""If $1,600 is not sufficient, you are at liberty to indulge in private work."" The wreck commissioner is necessarily a seafaring man, and a seafaring man is not very likely to be readily capable of adapting himself to some other occupation such as that of a stockbroker or a druggist. His only natural occupation must be in connection with seafaring matters, such as surveying, the testing of compasses, and so on. I am not saying that this man did such work, because I do not know, and I am going to be very conservative in my statements. But I do know that the regulations of the department under which he was employed permit him, if he so wishes, to engage in private work. Now, that is worse than if a judge were given a beggarly salary and told that he might go out and engage in legal work on the side, because a judge might do a great deal of legal work and yet never come in contact with his clients in the court over which he presided. Moreover, if there were any likelihood of that happening, he could get a brother judge to take his case. But this man is sole judge of these cases on the Pacific coast, and more than that, his clientele, if I may use the word, is limited. The number of men engaged in seafaring pursuits on the Pacific coast of British Columbia, that is, those who own boats there, is extremely limited, and if this man is to get employment, as he is invited to do by the government regulations, he must seek it from among the very men on whom he may sit to-morrow in judgment in connection with very important matters indeed. He must be familiar with all these men; he must be on friendly terms with them if he wants to get employment from them, yet he is put in the position of working for them one day and sitting in judgment on them the next. I do not say he ever did any such private work, because, as I have said, I do not know; but I submit that it is an undesirable position for the government regulations to create.

The government will say, no doubt, and say very truly, that the work offering on that coast in this connection is not large enough to justify the payment of a proper salary to a man who should devote his whole attention to it. Well, in that case it would be far better to close the office and either send a man from this coast to deal with the specific cases, or else put them in the hands of the judge in admiralty. There is a Supreme Court judge there who has made a lifelong study of admiralty matters; he sits as admiralty judge when occa-

sion demands, and he has the advantage of being able to judge evidence properly, which no man not of the legal profession has the ability to do; moreover, he would be absolutely independent. Take whichever position you like, whether you send a man from here or whether you put the cases in the hands of the admiralty court there, it is highly desirable that the man who sits in judgment on these cases, who sits alone and has to deal with matters veiy technical and difficult in their character, should not have affiliations of a business or social or personal character with the men on whom he sits in judgment or the interests involved in the cases which come before him. I think that is absolutely incontrovertible, and so far as the government's responsibility goes, I suggest that they look into that aspect of it.

I do not suggest that this wreck commissioner was corrupt, nor do I intend, having safeguarded myself, so to speak, by that statement, to go on and by hint or innuendo suggest that he was corrupt, because I do not think so; if I did I would say so. But I do suggest that this evidence shows that he was very careless or very incompetent, or both. My opinion is that he was both. The evidence shows-and I am prepared to give the book and page for every one of these statements, but I will not detain the House; I will simply make the statements-that almost from the beginning of the case he was prejudiced in favour of the decision which he ultimately gave. He was partial in the bringing out of the evidence; he did not give the evidence its proper value, and he did not obtain evidence that was very material; evidence that was most vital was practically omitted. I wish to state again that I do not know any of the parties to the dispute. The only person I know in connection with it was a constable who was only a minor witness. I know none of these men personally or by repute other than as recorded in the pages of the sworn evidence taken in the course of the investigation. I will give you a short history of the case and later on I will refer to the lack of material evidence, and I think it will be admitted that what I say in this respect is correct.

I will give you a short history of the first trip, and I will give it to you from the evidence of men who were there, disinterested men who made the trip in their capacities as engineer or fireman, men who were not interested in the company and who had nothing to gain by telling the truth or otherwise. I cannot give you the history of the second trip, except as to its initial stages, because everybody was lost. One of the principal
Sup-ply-Marine-The Alaskan

witnesses was a Mr. Wilson, and the commissioner himself comments on the fair and frank way he gave his evidence. Wilson was an engineer; he had a first class Board of Trade certificate from the Old Country, and those of us who are familiar with the Board of Trade regulations in the Old Country know that that means he was a thoroughly competent engineer. He had had thirty years' experience ; which shows that he was a thoroughly experienced man. He got a position as engineer to make his first trip from Victoria to Barkley sound. He went down and took a glimpse at the boiler. He asked the captain if the boiler had been inspected, and was answered in the negative, whereupon he said, ""I am not going to sea until that boiler is inspected."" The captain said, ""Well, now, do not make any trouble; we have our charter and we want to go out. The boat is all right; the engine is all right; let us go out."" The engineer said, however, ""I am not going until I have inspected this boiler,"" and when he put it like that, they said, ""All right; go and look at the boiler."" So he took the top off it, or proceeded by whatever method is followed in such cases, and he found that there were four tubes missing, and four plugged-it was a water tube boiler-and that seven more were leaking. They were leaking with a pressure of cold water on the Victoria water system, which means about 80 or 90 pounds pressure. Of course, you need a higher pressure than that to run an engine, but with that pressure he found seven tubes leaking as well as eight that were out of business. He also found that several of the pumps were in bad shape, valves missing and packing gone, and that there were no wrenches with which to fix the pumps; it is recorded here that he had to send up town to buy some wrenches for the purpose. Mind you, this was a boat going out on the open Pacific in mid-winter, yet they had not enough wrenches with which to fix the pumps, and if he had not insisted on this investigation before they started they would have gone out with the pumps not working and with no tools available to make the necessary adjustments or repairs. After they had fixed the boat up-and he tells us they spent three days tinkering on it; they had no machine shop available-as he himself said, ""We decided to make the trip."" They started out, I understand, about one-thirty in the afternoon, and they bad not gone very far ""when we found the bilges flooding, and the pumps were choked; so we put into Beachy bay,"" which is fourteen miles from Victoria. Now these pumps had been tinkered with before they started, and they had proceeded only

fourteen miles when this trouble occurred. Fortunately, they found a place where they could put in-it is not generally the case on the west coast that such a place can conveniently or readily be found. They put in at Beachy bay and spent all night fixing up the pumps.

Apparently they were satisfied then, and they started out again the next morning. They had not gone very far, I suppose about forty miles further, when they found there was no water in the boiler, and as you know, you need water to make steam, and if you have no water you cannot go very far. They were liable to drift on the rocks around Pachena Point, and the engineer in his log says that he had to use salt water for keeping up steam, which has about the same effect as if you used salt water for oiling a car in order to get a mile or two more out of her and reach safety. ""I am afraid the old kettle won't stand it,"" the engineer says in his log. They altered their course; instead of going to Kildonan they went to Bamfield, which was the nearest place where they could get water and a sheltered place. The salt water which the engineer had used did enable them to get to Bamfield. They got water there and started off to their destination, which was about ten miles distant. They got there under these conditions, and incidentally I may say they struck the wharf going in and damaged it. ""Not enough power"" was the reason given. When they raised steam again the engineer had to take the top off the boiler and cut six more tubes out on account of the damage done by the salt water, making ten short out of about fifty. This all took time and in the meantime the boat was being towed around by some local boat so that they could get their cargo of fish on board. After some days they started out with a load and the first thing that happened was that the boat was on fire. The owners at the investigation described it casually as ""a little scorching"" but the engineer said in his evidence that it was enough to break the glass in the pilot house. That is where you stand to steer; it is the only place where you can steer from, and if the fire was bad enough to break the glass in the pilot house it would not have needed to get a great deal worse before it would have been impossible for them to steer the boat at all. On that occasion it was due to the shifting of the baffle-plates-I do not want to be too technical, but I cannot but be technical just here. I gather from the evidence that these baffle-plates are put on top of the tubes to prevent the heat rushing out too violently into the
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

funnel, something like a damper on a stove. These baffle-plates had got loose and the funnel got so hot that it set fire to the woodwork of the pilot house in the vicinity. They got the fire put out and fixed up the baffle-plates as well as they could. They did not stop to do that, but did it as they went along.

Next they had such a big load on, not only in the interior but also on the deck, that they noticed the deck buckled a bit and the doors jammed. The owner of the boat denied that, but he was not there, and this man who was there says he saw the deck buckled. They went on again and presently they found there was no water in the boiler, and the engineer said in his evidence ""I was scared to take a chance by putting more salt water in. I was afraid she would burst or scald someone."" So the weather being fine-it was smooth water and a very fine day for the time of year-she drifted around in the straits from eight in the morning till two in the afternoon. Less than half of that time would have sufficed to send her ashore and wreck her if the weather had been at all stormy, but fortunately the weather was smooth. Then a United States cruiser came along and gave her water. Then she started out again between two and three and by four o'clock they were out of water again. They drifted around in the dark until nine o'clock when the C.P.R. steamer the Tees came along and offered her a tow. They hitched on to the bitts, which is an iron frame fastened to the decks and is generally used to fasten the rope to when the boat is moored alongside the wharf. They hitched on to one of the bitts and in ten minutes had pulled it out. Then they pulled out the other one, and as the engineer said ""The wood looked to be pretty rotten where it came out."" The Tees came back again for another trial and hitched on to the mast. That stood, and finally they reached Victoria with water on the engine room floor. They managed to get to Victoria, which was not their destination, but Vancouver. There they overhauled the pumps. Three had no packing, and then they discovered why they had no water. There was a leaking pipe between the water cistern and the boiler, so they put a new cistern on the deck and that enabled them to get to Vancouver, their destination. They then put her into a repair place for repairs, and they took up this pipe and found that it was a two-inch galvanized iron pipe, and in the language of the engineer ""it was pretty well rotten."" They had to move the floor to get at this pipe; otherwise it could not be seen. This boat was supposed to be in first-class shape

when she left, but this pipe had neither been tested nor examined. The owner gave as a reason in his evidence that he thought some time it must have been frozen, and then of course that would make a leak, and rust would follow after that. But the boat was supposed to be in first class condition and you could not look at this pipe without tearing up a little bit of the deck. This boat went to sea in a condition which I think I can show ultimately resulted in its loss.

The engineer then recommended a new boiler or re-tubing the old one, but his recommendation w^s not accepted. Then he said, ""I am not going back to sea in that boat unless she is re-tubed or a new boiler put in."" He was getting good pay and times were bad, but he told one of the assessors at this examination that he would not be a bit surprised considering the condition of the boiler to hear that something had gone wrong in rough weather. He was pressed to say what he thought caused the loss, and he replied that it must either have shipped a sea into the engine room or else a tube burst in the boiler. The sea could only come into the engine room through the doors and shutters, and there were the usual doors to prevent that. So it is more logical to take his other reason as being the correct one, that the tubes had burst.

It leaks gradually and it will be days or weeks before it becomes dangerous, but on account of salt water being used
