in the boiler, patches of it would crust small pieces the size, say, of a five-cent piece at certain corners and elbows, and that would prevent water getting at the tube, and then the piece would burn out and the tube would burst and the water in all the tubes would run into the fire box and put out the fire. It was more dangerous on account of having used the salt water. The engineer was pressed to say that things were not as bad as he had said. He was asked, ""After these repairs, don't you think she was all right?"" The engineer replied, ""After the repairs I would not have gone myself,"" and he did not go. He quit his job rather than go. That completes the history of the first voyage. I might mention that in leaving that wharf she knocked down six more piles. The reason was that she had too much power. On her way to Victoria she went on fire again, but that is part of the second trip. It sounds like a jest, does it not, but it is the solemn truth as revealed by sworn evidence.

That is the history of the first trip of that boat on the strength of statements made by reliable witnesses, the engineer and his assistant, dependable men who had certificates which they were liable to lose if they made a false statement. This testimony is better, in my opinion, than the interested statements of the owners, who sat back in their offices in Victoria and Vancouver and ""thought and believed and supposed"" for that is the tenor of most of their evidence if you subject it to a close scrutiny. Whatever evidence they had to support them was either from employees or firms that they had business contracts with as I will explain later on. Now, the distance from Victoria to Kildonan is roughly 130 miles so we have this situation: Here is a boat in a first class condition-or supposed to be. After having been further overhauled by her engineer and his assistant, she does not get 14 miles before she has to lie up all night to make repairs on her pumps. The next day she had to use salt water; she struck a wharf; she was towed around while being repaired. She starts out with so heavy a deck load that the deck buckles. Then she went on fire enough to break the glass in the pilot house. She breaks down and drifts in the open strait. She starts off again and again breaks down and drifts for five hours in the dark. She is picked up again and the tow tears out both bitts because the wood is pretty rotten, and at last crawls into Victoria with water on the engine room floor. And this was all in a trip of 130 miles, less than 300 miles on the round trip and most of it in sheltered water. What would have happened,

I wonder, if she had gone down as far as Seattle or San Francisco where she would have been exposed during the whole trip to the buffeting of the Pacific ocean? I would like to quote here the view the commissioner takes of the incidents that I have described without a word of exaggeration. Here is how he dismisses all that. Addressing one of the principal owners he says:
There is no doubt you had completed one voyage and, apart from little accidents it was completed successfully. A. Yes, sir.

Apart from ""little accidents,"" Mr. Chairman, it was completed successfully! If it was not such a dreadful tragedy it would be too comical. It reminds one of the Apostle Paul and the boasting he did in his elderly garrulity, that he had been so many times beaten and put in gaol, that he had been stoned, that he had been shipwrecked three times, and had been in the deep for a day and a half. That, however, was the record of a life time of adventure. This happened in a week onlv!

Now to go on to the next trip. Unfortunately it was lamentably short because the vessel and crew were lost very soon after they started out. They started out from Vancouver and, as I say, knocked out six piles of the wharf. Seemingly the vessel had too much power. She went on fire on her way to Victoria and her baffle plates again shifted. Now the journey from Victoria to Vancouver is in inside waters therefore the vessel did not encounter any heavy seas calculated to bring about a shaking which would have caused these baffle plates to shift. The plates were fixed in Victoria and the vessel started out at eight p.m., but returned again at two a.m.-""too hot."" Finally a man was got from Vancouver to fix the baffle plates. Presumably they were fixed properly because we heard no more about it. The vessel loaded a cargo of box lumber and started off again in absolutely calm weather; the meteorological conditions show that. She was next seen off Pachena Point thirty hours after she had left Victoria. Now Pachena is about seventy miles from Victoria and the vessel was able to do six or seven knots an hour. So that in ordinary fair weather she should have made that distance in about eleven hours. Instead of that she occupied thirty hours. Where was she during the nineteen hours which intervened? We have no record to show that, no one can tell. She must have spent those nineteen hours somewhere between Victoria and Pachena Point. We have no way of knowing what happened. Did she go into Beach bay to fix up her baffle plates, or did more tubes burst and were
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

efforts made to carry out repairs? No one can tell. What we do know is that she delayed somewhere for nineteen hours before she was seen off Pachena Point. The vessel was next seen at 3.30 p.m., by the lighthouse keeper, passed Pachena Point and heading towards cape Beale which was 6 or 7 miles distant and had she rounded that point she would have been in sheltered water. If there was a very strong wind and a heavy sea running from the start of the trip one could understand what had happened. But the meteorological report shows that the wind during the time was only moderate. It was not until afterwards that what might be described as a strong gale sprang up. So that during the nineteen hours referred to the vessel could and should have reached a place of safety long before the wind increased in violence. Anyhow the centre of the gale was some 200 miles north so that she would not have experienced the worst end of it. When first sighted by the lighthouse keeper the vessel was going very slowly but was too close in; she was either steaming or drifting towards shore. Now, if either a steamship or a sailing boat is near the shore in a heavy wind the first precaution to be observed is to get off that shore. It is therefore reasonable to assume that if this vessel was capable of steaming she would have changed her course, she would have steamed away from that shore and reached a place of safety because there was a harbour of refuge only a few miles away. But as the lighthouse keeper says she kept steaming or drifting to the shore.

Now, I think here is one of the most significant facts as to what really caused the loss of this boat. She was watched closely by the lighthouse keeper, or his wife, and during all that time, between then and dark, they saw no sign of steaming; no sign of smoke coming out of the funnel. The vessel was only a mile and a half away. In British Columbia they use bituminous coal and what is called ""run of the mine"" for steamships. This contains a great deal of slack and I can certify myself that it makes a very strong, black smoke. You can easily see it for quite a distance; I am well within the mark when I say that it is readily discernible at a distance of ten miles. This vessel was only a mile and a half away. It was being watched by somebody whose attention was called to the danger the boat was in and he swears that he saw no sign of smoke coming out of the funnel. Had that boat been in a condition to steam the onlooker would certainly have seen smoke belching out of her funnel. Every-

body on board having been lost it is impossible that we shall ever ascertain the facts; but I suggest it is probable that a tube burst in her boiler and the vessel drifted around while her crew were trying to get it fixed up. At any rate with this vessel not steaming within a mile and a half of the rocks and a strong wind blowing towards the shore we can know exactly what was going to happen-If that was not the cause what did happen? There is no other suggestion that is tenable.

I may mention that the practice when a vessel becomes disabled at sea is to send up a flare or other signal of distress. The watcher in the lighthouse continued to observe the motions of the boat until after it became dark and observed the crew put up several flares. It shows that the vessel was not abandoned-although someone suggested that she had been-that there were men on board and that they were not able to leave.

Now we have had the evidence before the Commission of Inquiry of some of the government inspectors who I think, came out very well, in regard to their actions in connection with the matter. Inspector Stevens, of Vancouver, speaks as follows and this is a vital point. He was asked if, when this boat was repaired, he should not have been informed of the fact and he said ""absolutely."" The examination continues:
Q. They should have notified you.-A. Yes. The act
says so. I think it is section 591 or 624 where it says that the owners, masters or engineers should report to the steamboat inspector.
Q. They did not comply with that law?-A. If there was any damage to the boiler they should have notified us.
Q. Supposing the ship had been repaired?-A. If she had been repaired, there must have been some damage.
Q. And they should have notified you?-A. Absolutely.
And then he quotes the section of the act.

If that notification had been given and if the inspector had come down and glanced over the condition of that boiler, I am safe in saying that the boat would never have gone out till her tubes had been repaired, and the salt water conditions made right. He did not know of her condition and was not supposed to know. The boat had suffered damage and it was their duty to report. I have looked up the act and I know the provisions in regard to it, and I say it was the duty of the owners to give notice. It was not so much because of what had been done in the way -of repairs, but it was the safeguard; the inspector would have gone down and examined the boiler and said ""That boat must never leave port till it is properly repaired."" That was the only safeguard the crew had, and it
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

is for that reason I hold the owners responsible. I think there were four owners and one of them said he was an engineer. Therefore, he should have known what the law was. He said all the necessary things were done. He said in his evidence that the boat had been inspected and overhauled, but it is a fact that this inspector was not notified of these repairs.

Then again Inspector Cullam of Victoria happened to be coming along the street and saw the boat preparing to go out without any lifeboat. He rang up the owners and said ""You cannot go out without a lifeboat."" The owner approached the captain and tried to excuse it, and said ""Do not make a fuss about it, it will be all right next trip, we have a nice little boat; come down and look at it, it will be all right."" But Mr. Cullam, with admirable determination said ""It is not all right; you do not go out with that dinky little boat, you must get a proper lifeboat."" So alert was he that he telephoned the collector of customs and said ""Do not let that boat go out until you get a permit from me."" He thought they would try to go out in spite of his instructions, but he adhered to his determination and they had to get a proper lifeboat on that occasion.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. NEILL; Earlier in my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I said that among the faults I found with the investigation which we are considering was the fact that, as I believe, material evidence had not been adduced that could have been procured. I want to deal with that matter for a moment. The man from whose evidence I have been principally quoting, Wilson, was on the first trip of the boat, but he did not go out on the second. There were also a number of other men who, warned by the experiences which I narrated this afternoon, decided as well to quit the boat. None of these men were called; but there was one man in particular who undoubtedly should have been called, and that was Brock. He was the captain on the first trip; in fact, he owned the boat, having bought it under option from the vendors. He had bought it from them and had endeavoured to sell shares in it to various friends of his, among whom was a practical engineer named Redding. Redding canned the idea promptly, having given one look at the engines; but

Brock went on the first trip of the boat, and on his return, Mr. Redding, who gave evidence at the investigation, meeting him, congratulated him on having escaped with his' life; and Brock replied: ""Yes, I saw the rats leaving the ship in Victoria and thought it was time to quit."" Now, that statement might be taken in its literal sense, that Brock actually saw rats leaving the ship; but I take it that what he really meant was that, in view of the condition of the ship and the engines, he 'bought it was time to leave it, and that was why he did not go on the second trip. But, [DOT]Sir, I wanted to submit, Redding's evidence for this reason: he was asked several questions about the man Brock, who did not appear to be on the horizon at all. Amongst other questions, this one was put to him by one of the assessors:
My question is, can he-
That is, Redding.
-say whether Brock is out for the time being while the investigation is on?
That is to say, in other words, was he hiding or keeping out of the way? The answer made by the witness was:

It is a question I would sooner leave unanswered. That answer, I think, would naturally suggest to any of us the idea that it was highly desirable to procure the evidence of a man of whom it was at least implied that he might be keeping out of the way until the investigation was over. And the commissioner himself said: ""We ought to have Mr. Brock's evidence."" But what means did he employ to get Brock? He asked Mr. Wright, one of the owners of the boat, to get him; and if there is any truth in the suggestion that Brock was keeping, or was being kept, out of the way on purpose, Wright was the very man who was interested in seeing that he did not come to court. The commissioner entrusted to him the duty, or rather the business-because it was not his duty-to procure Brock in order that he might give evidence possibly against his interests; and the consequence, which I think was not unnatural, was that Brock did not appear. Nothing appears in the evidence to show why he was not procured, but I am told by a man who was present that the question was brought up on the last day of the investigation. The question was asked where Brock was, or why he did not come to give evidence, and the reply was made that he was at Powell river and had no money to come in. I do not know what the mileage would be, but at any rate it would not cost more than five or six
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

dollars for boat fare from Powell river to Vancouver; and the assertion that Brook had no money to come down from Powell river, and that therefore on that account his evidence was not available, was not, in my opinion, by any means satisfactory. I submit that that fact alone betrays the very strongest, I will not say suspicion-yes, I will say that; ""suspicion"" is the right word-suspicion of the competency of the court as conducted. It is absolutely inexcusable that the man who was the captain of the boat on the previous trip, in regard to whom the suggestion was made that he was keeping out of the way on purpose, and who was ordered to be brought forward for examination, should fail to appear, solely for the trumpery reason that he had no money to pay his fare. It was not the business of those in charge of the investigation to be satisfied with that bald statement, for the money could have been easily procured to bring him into court; and failure to procure him is unjustifiable and inexcusable from any point of view that can be taken.

There is another point which I would submit to the committee. One of the witnesses swore in the presence of the owner of the boat, or at least one of the owners of the boat, that it was so heavily laden that it buckled with the weight. The owner of the boat denied that, but still the assertion was mad'e. On her first trip from Barkley sound to Vancouver she had a cargo of fish in boxes, no doubt consigned to various people in Vancouver. It would have been easy to ascertain the weight of that cargo, the invoices would have shown the number of boxes and their weight, and from this data they would have had a good idea whether she was overloaded to the extent of buckling her deck. Then again, no attempt was made to follow up that line of inquiry. On her second trip she was loaded with what are called box shooks, that is, fish boxes knocked down, four feet long one foot wide and one inch deep. They were piled up on deck, and the evidence showed there had not been the slightest attempt made to fasten the deck load by any means whatever. Thus you had this boat going out into the heavy sea with a lot of loose lumber on her deck, and every wave that broke overboard would lift two or three of the top shooks and wash them overboard with any member of the crew who might be standing on them. It would have been easy to ascertain from the stevedoring company how she was loaded- whether this cargo was thrown on like a heap

of firewood, or whether any attempt was made to secure the deck load from being washed overboard. Even a vessel going out with a deck load of heavy timbers has these properly secured so that they will not be affected by heavy seas. But there was no attempt made to find out how the Alaskan was loaded, whether she was properly loaded or whether she was overloaded-information which could have been easily ascertained from the stevedoring company who loaded her in Victoria.

There is another serious failure on the part of the wreck commissioners; they did not visit the scene of the wreck. Suppose this House burned down to-morrow, and we had two commissioners engaged from Toronto to make an investigation, what would we think of them if, instead of visiting Ottawa and inspecting the scene of the fire, they proceeded to Winnipeg and held their inquiry there? The reason given by the commissioner was that the scene of the wreck was remote and difficult to get at. In reply to this, I may say that there is a well-equipped Canadian Pacific passenger boat which goes three times a month within eleven miles of the spot, and from there to the wreck is a comparatively easy walk over a trail. It would have been a rough walk and in wet weather rather unpleasant, but a woman made the trip the day after the wreck, and there was nothing to prevent any able-bodied men visiting the scene of the wreck, where they would have learned a good deal of very great value in the investigation. I may say that the coroner's inquest which sat upon one of the men's bodies that drifted ashore had no difficulty whatever in visiting the place. If the commissioners had visited the wreck perhaps we would have found in the annex to their report a definite statement as to whether the wreck was that of the Alaskan or not. Doubt is expressed as to whether the wreckage found belonged to the Alaskan or not, but there were reasons for that expression of doubt, as I shall show. But had they visited the scene of the wreck it would have been impossible for them to express any such doubt. The evidence showed there had been no wreck for ten years within ten miles of either side of the wreck found there. We have the small shallow bay there practically covered with this shook lumber-the cargo of the Alaskan-drifting all around; we have a lifeboat found there with the name ""Vancouver"" and corresponding with the boat purchased by the owners for the Alaskan; we have a number of life belts washed ashore with the name of the Alaskan on them; we have the body of a man, identified as one of the crew, cast ashore
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

at this place. Yet this commission that sat one hundred and fifty miles away found it impossible to say whether or not that was the wreck of the Alaskan. There was also a piece of wreckage thirty feet long and, I think, ten or twelve feet across-I forget the exact measurement-and its condition was such that it was highly desirable not to connect it up with the Alaskan, which perhaps was the reason that this dubiety was expressed. A piece produced by one of the witnesses-a constable, totally disinterested, having no connection with any of the parties-was so rotten that he said he had kicked it off the main piece of the wreck. Those interested tried to make out that it was not part of the wrecked Alaskan, but I think there can be no doubt it was. The coroner's inquest at least had no trouble in finding that this was the wreck. Their verdict in part reads as follows:
That the wreckage of the ss. Alaskan, as examined by them, was very old and rotten.

They had no doubt, having seen the wreckage, whether it was part of the Alaskan or not, and had this commission, as they could easily have done, visited the place they would not have had any doubts either.

There is another matter. A chain was discovered at the wreck about thirty or forty feet long. An attempt was made by the owners of the boat to suggest that it was a piece of old chain that had been lying on the boat deck for casual purposes; but that suggestion was destroyed by the evidence of one of the witnesses who swore it was attached to this piece of wreckage thirty feet long by twelve feet wide found at the spot. Next an attempt was made to suggest that it was a stay chain used for staying the mast, but further investigation proved that a stay chain in that particular place for that particular purpose would not exceed six feet in length. But it was imperative to prove that this chain had nothing to do with the Alaskan, and they next brought somebody into court who swore positively that the chain was not on the boat. On cross-examination, however, it developed that he had not seen the boat for three years, so that weakened his assertion very much. Now, I have here a small piece of that chain, and I will send it over to the members of the government so they can see how worn and weak it is. One end is broken off altogether, and some of the links are about the thickness of a sheet of paper. The constable said that this short piece was a fair sample of the thirty or forty- [DOT] foot length. Some of the evidence went to suggest that the chain was the steering gear of

the boat; but that is not so. From other evidence it appears that this was the limber chain. I am not going into a technical explanation. I need only say that such a chain is used in keeping the openings clear for the water to reach the pump, and if the chain breaks the water is very liable to fill up in the bilges and flood the boat. Whatever purpose this chain was used for, it is a sample of what was considered sufficient for the equipment of that boat. There is a saying that you can judge the unknown by the known. Well, there is something we can look at, at any rate, and so get an idea of the rest of the equipment. There is no question whatever that that was part of the equipment of the Alaskan.
Now, I want to quote briefly a few remarks by the lawyer who represented the relatives of one of the drowned men, the captain of the boat. Here are some of his remarks:
Mr. MacTaggart: I think it is quite clear from the evidence that if there had been any survivors the owners would have been called upon to answer in another court. The evidence shows that.
Further on he says:
In my opinion this investigation should have taken place at Pachena-
That is where the wreck occurred.

-and it could have been ascertained in ten minutes how she broke up and possibly how she was wrecked. If you believe the evidence of the men from the west coast that the large piece they found was a part of the Alaskan and that a piece was kicked off it by their feet, it show's what the condition of this vessel was. Mr. Gordon tells you that there was no other wreckage there and that, therefore, this must have been a part of the wreck of the Alaskan. Unless it is thought that these men came here to perjure themselves, their evidence must be accepted. It is a matter for your consideration. I maintain that that (indicating) is a representative piece of the hull of the Alaskan and, if that is so, it is quite time that there was inspection of the hull for vessels of 150 tons or less.

I quite agree with his remarks in regard to that. I want to quote for a moment the annex to the report. There was a short report saying the wreck was due to a gale, and then the annex goes into more detail. In the annex the question appears:
Was this boat when she left Victoria in good seaworthy condition?
And the answer given is as follows:

From the evidence of reputable persons in the employ of her former owners, the Pacific Salvage Company Limited, of Victoria, of responsible employees of Messrs. Yarrows Limited, shipbuilders, etc., of Esquimalt, B.C., as also other witnesses, the vessel when she left Victoria, B.C. on the 1st January, 1923, was * as regards her hull and equipment seaworthy, etc.
You will note the expression: ""From the evidence of reputable persons."" No doubt
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

they were reputable-I do not suggest these men meant to perjure themselves at all-but who were they? Every man jack of them was interested. They were either the owners of the vessel, or they were the late owners who were in a sense interested, because it was asserted that they had O.K.'d her staunchness to the new purchasers. And the other people, the Yarrows and so on, they were shipbuilders, people who had contracts for the repair of this and similar boats, and who hoped to get more contracts in the future. As I say, they did not go there to perjure themselves, but they certainly went there to give as favourable evidence as possible for the owners. There is keen competition among shipbuilders, and naturally they are not going to injure their clients if they can help it, that is, if they can put things in as favourable a light as possible consistent with truth. You can make truth look a good deal nicer if you want to than if you do not; there is no question about that. The head manager of this salvage company, the late owners, who was trying to do the best he could for his friends, admitted on cross-examination that in all the six or seven years that they had the boat they had never let her go outside-""outside"" means into outside waters. They had kept her inside, in smooth waters; that was his experience of the best way to handle that boat. We must compare the evidence of these interested people with the evidence of this engineer, who had no axe to grind; with the evidence of government officials, who were equally trustworthy; and I think I am right in saying that the evidence of these disinterested parties should have been accepted or should at least have been given more weight than the evidence of those who were clearly interested, directly or indirectly.
Then, I refer again to their report, from where I was reading before. It says:
They found that the whole equipment was seaworthy but manifestly was unsafe to venture on such a voyage in such conditions of weather as existed at the time of her loss.

Now, the dictionary meaning of ""seaworthy"" is ""fit or safe to go to sea;"" so it would appear that this boat was fit and safe to go to sea but manifestly was unsafe to go if it went outside the harbour. Well, if a boat is fit to go to sea one must assume that it will be fit to encounter a reasonable degree of weather; I think there is no question about that. But they go on record as saying that the boat was seaworthy but manifestly unsafe to go to sea- there is the plain English of it-unsafe to go away from the inside harbour.
I am well aware that the loss of ships at sea is due either to foundering as the result of

a heavy gale-swamping, in fact-or to a breakdown which puts the ship at the mercy of the sea and causes it very soon to go to pieces. This boat did not founder at sea, because she was seen drifting on to the rocks; therefore she met with some mishap; she became disabled. That disablement could not have been connected with her sailing abilities, because she had none; it must therefore, have been connected with her steaming abilities. I suggest that the reason was that her engines became disabled through the fact that one of these tubes to which I have alluded burst and had put out the fire, and there was no more steam available.

Turning again to the report, we find it stated that the condition of the machinery was ""very good""-and that in the face of the facts that I have mentioned-and that ""the boiler, however, would probably have had to have considerable attention paid to it at her next annual inspection."" In the face of all the facts I have laid before the House-that this man gave up a job worth $200 a month rather than risk his life on the boat again; that he warned them that the boiler ought to be retubed; that they had given orders to the marine repair shops to be ready for them on a future ocasion; that a man named McGrath heard the captain say to one of the owners that ""she ought to have been fixed up before, but we had not enough money and she will have to run a trip or two more before we can afford to do it""-notwithstanding all these facts, which are in the evidence, you have it solemnly stated that the boat was ""very good,"" but she would probably have to have some overhauling in the near future.

To sum up the situation, we find this little bunch of would-be quick millionaires buying this boat on a shoe-string at $6,000-and insuring her immediately for 50 per cent more; we find them buying this rotten old hull that had not been inspected by the government for thirty-six years. We have them making this trip with all the accidents that the commissioner refers to as ""little accidents,'' but which, perhaps, have a greater significance in view of what took place on tho next trip. We find them cautioned and advised by their engineer, who said he would not go to sea; that he would quit rather than take the risk on it again, and also that there was an utter disregard of the regulations, which provided that in a case of that kind they should report these repairs to the inspector of boilers. We find them trying to .go out of Victoria harbour without a lifeboat, and when called to question we find them offering an excuse and saying they would put
Supply-Marine-The Alaskan

one on on t)he next trip. We find that one of the principal owners was an engineer, who knew or should have known what the regulations were. But they went out without reporting these repairs; they tried to go out without a lifeboat-in other words, they took a gamble, not with their own money and then own lives, but with the lives of the crew; for that was the stake, that was the issue. Unfortunately the boat was lost; they lost their bet-and who paid for it? Not the men who should have paid, not the men who would have got the benefit if they had won their bet, not the men who would have reaped the profits, but the unfortunate crew. It was they who paid for it; and their widows and children-one of them left six small children-will be paying for it for ten yearn to come in a life of poverty and, no doubt, insufficient educational facilities. But the owners of the boat-they do not have to pay for it; they will get their $9,000 of insurance where they paid only $6,000 for the boat. They will get their insurance money, which, I think, would be well described as blood money, for that is practically what it comes to. And I note that the price of blood has increased of late years. Judas Iscariot got thirty pieces of silver for betraying innocent blood, but my friends here were going to get, over and above the cost of the boat, three thousand pieces of silver for betraying the lives of eleven men. I notice that Judas Iscariot at least became repentant and tried to undo what he had done by giving back his blood money, but I do not see any sign of that in this case. I do not hear any word of this $3,000 of profit, profit by mens' lives, being handed over to the widows and children. No; they will collect their money and look for another boat to finance on a shoe-string as before, no doubt.

I am not talking simply for the sake of informing the House; I have one or two definite suggestions to make. These men are liable to a heavy fine under the act-I need not quote it; section 591, I think it is-for not reporting these repairs. I maintain that had these repairs been reported the engineer would never in God's world have let that boat go out in the condition she was in. The trivial repairs they did make-the tinkering- had they been reported according to law, these men would have been alive to-day. I suggest to the government, therefore, that in the ordinary course of business they should have these men prosecuted, not in any spirit of revenge-that would be a poor solace to the widows and children-but merely to impress upon them and to impress upon other ship

owners inclined to do the like that they muse not evade these regulations; that the regulations, apparently trivial, are intended for the preservation of life; that they are very important, and that they must be adhered to. The only way you can impress that on some people is by making them pay out of their own pockets. I suggest it is thoroughly proper and

column21: law.Now these men have been sacrificed. I perhaps was wrong in comparing the shipowners to Judas Iscariot because after all, his action was wilful and these men were not guilty of deliberately sending these men to their deaths. If they had known, I suppose they would not have done it, but they were guilty of this:
column22: They were guilty of risking these

column1: men's lives for selfish greed. Put it on the highest plane it was careless, selfish greed. They were willing to take a risk with somebody else's life. These men are gone. I do not want to go into any heroics about that, because nothing would be more out of keeping, but it is our duty if we can, to so consider the matter that these men shall not have lost their lives in vain. It might be some consolation to their widows if they knew that the loss of their husbands had drawn the attention of the government to the importance of having boats under 150 tons in burden inspected, and the men who work on this class of boats protected. Mj' suggestion is that the limit under which inspection should not be enforced should be reduced from 150. to say 75 or 50 tons. I want to be moderate in order to get the government to accept the situation. That would mean instead of a crew of eleven men, there would only be perhaps four or five endangering their lives in boats of this age and under these circumstances.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) when he was announcing in the House the other day the policy, and it was a very liberal policy I am glad to say, which he intended to inaugurate in connection with life-saving appliances on the west coast, when he came to this feature of reducing the inspection limit, hesitated and said that the matter was under the consideration of the government. It is for that reason I am bringing the matter up to-night so that the influence of these circumstances may induce the government to decide definitely that they will introduce legislation of that kind. It could be very easily done.

CANADA HIGHWAYS COMMISSION Ttpes or Road
There are six general types of road being constructed under federal aid judged from a ""surface"" stand point.

_ 1st. Cement Concrete Pavement.-Consists of a slab of Portland cement concrete from 6 inches to 8 j inches thick and having a crown of about 1 inch in ten feet. Transverse expansion joints one half inch wide are placed every 50 feet. The only base necessary for this type of pavement is a wall consolidated subgrade. Average cost per mile for this pavement 20 feet wide is $35,300.

2nd. Bituminous Concrete Pavement.-Consists of an intimate mixture of crushed stone, sand and bitumen laid 2 to 3 inches thick on a prepared base of cement concrete, waterbound macadam or well consolidated gravel. The aggregate is mixed at a high temperature in a special mixer and distributed and rolled while hot. Average costs per mile for this pavement 20 feet wide and 3 inches thick are as follows:-
On 5-inch waterbound macadam base
On 7-inch waterbound macadam base
On 4-inch cement concrete base
On 6-inch cement concrete base

3rd. Bituminous Macadam Penetration.-Consists of crushed stone spread on the road to a depth of 3 or 4 inches, lightly rolled then sprayed with hot bituminous binder, which flows into and penetrates the layer of stone. The whole surface is then sprinkled with small stone and consolidated by rolling, so that the binder fills the interstices between the stones. This pavement is usually laid on a waterbound macadam base. Average costs for 20 feet wide and 4 inches thick are as follows:-
On 5-inch waterbound macadam base
On 7-inch waterbound macadam base
On 8-inch waterbound macadam base

4th. Waterbound Macadam.-Consists of crushed stone spread on the roadway, filled with crusher screenings and consolidated by watering and rolling. It is usually laid in two courses (except when used as a base for hard top) and varies in total depth from 7 inches to 10 inches according to traffic requirements and condition of subgrade. This type of roadway is frequently finished with a top dressing of road oil and sand or oil and limestone chips, which preserves the surface, prevents ravelling and keeps down dust Average costs per mile are as follows,-
Oil treatment costs from $800 to $1,300 per mile in addition.

5th. Gravel Roadway.-Consists of a layer of gravel spread over the roadbed and consolidated by traffic or by rolling. It varies in thickness from 6 to 18 inches, depending on the character of the subgrade and the density of traffic. If the required thickness of gravel is greater than 6 inches it is usually laid in layers of 3 or 4 inches, each layer being consolidated before the next is applied.
The average cost of laying a gravel surface 20 ft. wide and 8 inches thick, based on a 2\ mile haul, is $4,700 per mile.

6th. Improved Earth.-This type of highway is formed by digging side ditches, throwing the material (such as it is) excavated therefrom onto the travelled way and grading it to a proper crown to shed water. Properly speaking the operation is one of grading and not of surfacing and usually provides a road which is good only in dry weather. If the material excavated from the side ditches happens to be gravel the road is a gravel road.
The cost varies with the size of ditch necessary to provide drainage and the range is from $1,000 to $4,000 per mile.
The above descriptions and costs apply only to the surfacing of roads. The construction of a highway involves other important and often costly operations, which may be described briefly as follows:-

1st. Clearing.-In constructing a new road through wooded country the first operation is that of cutting down and disposing of the trees and underbrush to the limits of the right of way and grubbing out roots where shallow cuts and fills are to be made.
Clearing costs from $200 to $4,000 per mile, depending on the size and density of the timber.

2nd. Grading.-This operation consists of forming the roadbed, which is to carry the finished surface. It involves the excavation of cuts and the filling of embankments, the protection of earth work from the action of rivers or lakes, the underdraining of wet places and the digging of ditches. The cost varies with the nature of the country, the nature of the material encountered, the allowable grade and the width of the roadbed to be constructed. The range is from $500 to $30,000 per mile.
3rd. Bridges.-This item covers the construction of all structures over 20 feet in clear span. The cost of such bridges may be anything from $500 to $500,000. Federal aid does not apply to such costs.

4th. Culverts.-The construction of all structures having a clear span of 20 feet or less, also pipes to carry streams across the roadway and under side entrance roads. Costs vary with the nature of the country, the number and size of streams and the type of culvert adopted. The range is from $500 to $10,000 per mile.
5th. Fencing.-Enclosing the right of way where necessary by fencing costs from $500 to $1,500 per mile.
6th. Tree Planting.-The growing shade of trees along the edge of the right of way protects the surface of the road from the extreme heat of the sun's rays in summer. This costs about $250 per mile.
7th. Miscellaneous.-The erection of crossing, danger and direction signs, guard rails, snow fences, etc Such items cost from nothing to $200 per mile.

666274,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.9.32,1923-05-28,717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a,ca.m.5259,Mr. COOTE:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,NOVA SCOTIA,,He may have put it a little strong, but at any rate that is what he said. Now, I want to point out very briefly one or two reasons why the government should give very careful consideration to the repre-sentatations made to them by the Minister of Agriculture. The Hon. Mr. Langley, when he appeared before the special Railway Transportation Cost committee a year ago, made this statement:
The impression is abroad among our farmers that the Board of Railway Commissioners has ceased to be a board of railway commissioners and has become a board of railway company commissioners.

That is a very serious statement, but I do not think it is at all too strong. I want to bring to the attention of the committee a few of the reasons why the people of western Canada feel just as Mr. Langley stated. On August 10, 1920, the Railway Commission commenced a hearing in Ottawa of an application of the railways for an increase in freight rates. That hearing was completed on August 21, and on September 9 there was put into effect the largest increase in rates that has ever been made in Canada,-an increase in the west of 35 per cent and in the east of 40 per cent. Now that was very quick work. There was no dissenting voice on the board, and certainly there was no delay. The increase was timed to catch the 1920 grain crop, and I believe that from my own station there were only seven carloads of grain shipped at the old rate. In my own particular town that increase took, I believe, out of the shippers of that one place a toll to the amount of $35,000. I would ask the

government to compare the ,speedy methods adopted in connection with this increase with the methods in regard to the decrease which was supposed to follow when circumstances would warrant. The officials of the United Farmers of Alberta went to the commission at Calgary on April 18, 1921, and asked permission to place before them their case for a reduction of rates, and at Regina on April 22, the Hon. George Langley and others appeared before the commission as representing the farmers of Saskatchewan. Representatives were also heard at Brandon, and, I think, at Winnipeg. During the summer of 1921 the United States railways cut the wages of their employees 12J per cent; and the Railway Commission of Canada of their own accord held an investigation to decide whether they could not now reduce these rates again. This investigation was carried on, I think, for a month and a half; but although the wages were reduced as I have said, some time previously,-in July, I think,-it was not until September 13 that Mr. Carvell issued a statement to the effect that all freight rates other than those on which reductions had already been made, should be decreased by 10 per cent from the increases given in 1920. This judgment was concurred in by Commissioner Nantel. Three of the commissioners dissented from the judgment because of the fact that the men had applied for a board of conciliation. I will not detain the House by reading anything in reference to this matter, but the fact remains that because these men had applied for a board three commissioners would not agree to the recommendation for a decrease in the rates which had been brought down by the Hon. Mr. Carvell on September 13. An agreement was arrived at between the Canadian Pacific Railway and their employees on October 8, by which the employees accepted a reduction. But these other gentlemen of the Railway Commission were so busy that they could not come to a decision in the matter at that time, and the reduction of this 10 per cent in the rates was not granted until November 23. Now, it does seem to the farmers of western Canada that the Railway Commission does not show any great desire to deal as quickly with an application for the lowering of rates as it does with any application for an increase. By November 23 the bulk of the grain had probably left the farmers' hands and the railways had got the increased rate.

One other thing I want to refer to, to show why the people of western Canada have lost all faith in the Board of Railway Commissioners as a fair judicial body. I might quote briefly from a report that appeared in the Calgary Herald of an address of the Hon. Mr
Supply-Railway Commission
Carvell before the Canadian Club. Referring to the increase which had been granted in the railway rates Mr. Carvell is reported as follows:

Mr. Carvell said that the railways had made representations to the Board of Railway Commissioners asking for an increase in rates and he said that it meant that $22,000,000 was required to pay the retroactive wages. The railways were hard put to it to pay this big increase. Three presidents of the railway companies came before the board and stated that if the money was not forthcoming there would be serious consequences and they were asked what they meant, and their reply was, it would mean a general strike of railway workers in Canada if the award was not agreed to.

In the same address Mr. Carvell stated that the demands in many cases were unreasonable. But he gives this threat of a strike as sufficient justification for raising the railway rates. He also stated that the farmer could sell his product in any market while the railway company could do business only on its rails and could not charge one cent more than the board allowed. If the Canadian Pacific Railway could not earn dividends no one would buy its shares, and as far as the McAdoo award was concerned, in four years this would have eaten up all the reserves of the company. He went on to dwell on the fact that the Canadian Pacific railway must have sufficient rates to earn their usual dividends.

At a hearing in Calgary on the following day, Mr. J. E. Brownlee, appearing for the United Farmers of Alberta, stated the farmers' case. He said that the farmers were forced to pay war prices for their needs but received only pre-war prices for their products, and this being the case they would probably cut down production to a considerable extent, and in that event any curtailment of transportation facilities would eventually work a hardship on the railway companies. Chief Commissioner Carvell scoffed at Mr. Brownlee's prediction. He is reported as having said:

Do not worry about the future, he said. I do not believe the farmers' organizations in the West are such half-dead, half-alive affairs as you hint. I do not believe there will be any lessening in production. Have a little more faith.

I should like the members of the government to compare the attitude exhibited by the Chairman of the Commission towards what we call ""capital"" and his attitude towards the common people, the producers of the country. He says that capital must have its 7 per cent or we cannot get it to build railways. And he holds out the threat of a strike on the part of the employees as justification for an increase in rates. Then when
the farmers threaten to curtail production, which is simply their method of striking, he says: ""Have a little more faith; do not worry about the future"".

Now, we have had a great deal of discussion in this House this session about emigration from this country, and we have been considering the problem of securing immigrants to take the places of those who leave. Well, I want to point out that just so long as we have men occupying high offices in this country-and I think that the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners holds one of the most important posts in the gift of the government-so long, I say, as there are in these high and important positions men who place more value on the dollar than they do on human life, we shall have before us an exceedingly difficult problem to keep people in this country to produce the material for the railways to haul; and it certainly is high time that there was a showdown as to who are to be given the primary consideration in Canada,-the people of the country or the people who are designated in the term ""capital"". I have no objection to the Canadian Pacific Railway getting dividends, but I do object that the Board of Railway Commissioners should act in a manner so manifestly unfair to one section of this country as the present board is doing. I want to quote from the words of the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners himself in a judgment given by him on September 15, 1920:

Allowing for the undoubted fact that a very large proportion of the traffic moved east and west is on a commodity basis, I am still forced to the conclusion that the rates in western Canada average considerably greater than in the East, possibly around 15 per cent to 18 per cent.

In the face of this remark from the chairman himself, I do not see why the people of western Canada cannot be granted an equalization of rates with the East. I think that the present chairman of the commission, in his refusal to grant such equalization, or at least to grant some redress to the people of the West is condemned by the words from his own mouth. I contend that there is nothing in the Railway Act by which it is intended that the Board of Railway Commissioners should maintain in western Canada rates 15 to 18 per cent higher than those that obtain in eastern Canada. If the Railway Commission want to maintain rates so that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company can continue to pay dividends in the future as they have in the past, their duty is to raise the rates in eastern Canada or lower them in
Supply-Railway Commission

western Canada until both eastern and western rates are on a parity. The people of the West are going to be satisfied with nothing less. The present Chairman of the Railway Commission may be very efficient but unless he can show better judgment in the future than he has done in the past, he cannot convince even honest people in eastern Canada of the fairness of the present condition of affairs.
Before I sit down I want to ask the minister one other question:
column2: Does the government

column1: think it is fair, although the major part of the Canadian Pacific Railway dividends are earned in western Canada, and rates are from 15 to 18 per cent higher there than in the East, that on a board composed of six commissioners there should not be one representative of western Canada? I hope that when the government give due consideration to the representations of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and possibly decide that the prseent chairman should be removed, they will give to western Canada one representative. I ask the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) will he be willing to go that far?

Rutherford was appointed as a western man to succeed a western man, and he is still a member of the Railway Board. I am not going to discuss the question of rates, it is too intricate, and, besides, I had something to do with perfecting the act under which the Board of Railway Commissioners was created. While this board may have made some mistakes at times-and I suppose even our judges are not entirely free from error-yet on the whole the work of the board has been excellent. Now, my hon. friend has mentioned the difference between eastern and western rates. I do not wish to make any comparisons in that way. It is the duty of the Board of Railway Commissioners to administer the Railway Act for the benefit of the whole Dominion, and I believe they are discharging this duty in a very able manner. Complaints regarding railway rates are not confined to the West; the people in the East complain that the rates from the Maritime provinces are very high and burdensome, and only to-day a question was brought up in the House as to a suggestion, I think, by some member of the government in New Brunswick, that the rates should be substantially reduced, and that unless something was done along this line the situation would be very serious indeed. The freight rate question is one of the disagreeable results of the war. No person can ever expect railway operation to be as cheap as it

was before the war. There is a new condition, and rightly so, among the working men of the Dominion, and, indeed, among the working men of the world; consequently, the wages of railway men will never revert to what they were before the war, and I do not think we want them to. The process of getting back to as near normal as possible will be comparatively slow. My hon. friend has said something about capital. Does he realize that he himself is one of the capitalists? The people of Canada own the biggest railway system in the world, every dollar of deficit on which has to be met out of the pockets of the taxpayers. The subject should always be approached with that in view. I appreciate the situation as to the freight rates, and I have sympathy not for the West any more than for the East, because all Canada is paying a very high freight rate and a very high passenger rate. But it will take some time for these rates to get down to normal. The only way we can get them to normal is to get a greater volume of traffic, and the only way to get a greater volume of traffic is to have more people to produce. It ought to be the object of us all to make Canada so far as population is concerned a bigger country, and to induce men to come here-notwithstanding all that has been said-to make for themselves and their families a future. I believe that in the proper solution of that one problem of immigration lies the remedy for most of our difficulties. As I say, I have great sympathy for my hon. friend and for both East and West in this matter. I am strongly in favour of reducing the rates as rapidly as possible so that the people who produce on the land and elsewhere will have a chance to get a greater return for their labours.

666280,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.9.38,1923-05-28,06b3ede1-7cd7-46e9-87f5-23c426b95e96,ca.m.4681,Mr. CAMPBELL:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,NOVA SCOTIA,,I do not want to get into a discussion on the immigration question because once that starts we do not know when it will end, but before this item passes I should like to say that before we start growing more grain we must have a reduction in the rates on grain or an increase in the price. Those of us who are farming in the West to-day know that it is an absurdity to think of growing more grain unless there is an improvement in conditions in some way or other. I do not like to discuss this rate problem from a western standpoint or an eastern standpoint, but from the Canadian standpoint. I have as much sympathy with the people of the Maritime provinces in their desire for a reduction of rates as I have with my own people in the West. I know conditions in that part of the country, and I know the people there have suffered a great deal. I am told on very good authority that last season no less than a million bushels of potatoes were spoiled in Prince Edward Island largely because there was not a sufficiently low rate to ship them out.

I think when we are discussing the responsibilities of the Railway Commission one of the troubles at least is that the commission has no control over a reduction of rates. I was reading a few days ago a pamphlet published, I think, by Mr. S. J. McLean, one of the Railway Commissioners, in which he stated he was surprised in looking over a
Supply-Railway Commission

number of tariffs to find that at least fifty per cent were apparently reductions in rates. That seems to tell us a good deal. We are demanding reductions on certain basic commodities-lumber, potatoes, grain, cattle and various other things-and yet all the time there are voluntary reductions taking place over which the commission has no control. That I say tells us a good deal. It seems to me there is a good deal of favouritism, that certain interests are getting special privileges in regard to freight rates, and the commission have no control over that whatever. Let me refer to just one product. Bar iron from Sydney. Nova Scotia, goes clean across the continent to Vancouver for sixty cents a hundred. I think that there is no hon. gentleman in this House who will say that the railway can carry that at a profit. It is patent that it must be carried at a distinct loss. That means that a railway company engaged in carrying that product for less than it costs must a short time afterwards come to the Railway Commission and ask for an increase in rates on something else, and that is precisely what is happening to-day.

I cannot agree with any suggestion of doing away with the Railway Commision or crippling its powers. I would rather be inclined to increase its powers. I think that the Commission should have control over the downward revision of rates. Why should a railway have authority to carry some product for less than it costs for some privileged interest, probably with some of its large shareholders interested in the railway, for that is practically what it is? J have been going over a lot of these figures, and I have found some of them illuminating. I have found some things that cannot possibly be justified.

Let me give another commodity. Rice from Vancouver is handled at seventy-five *cents a hundred to Calgary, yet that same rice is carried twenty-four hundred miles from there to Montreal for the same price; that means it is carried twenty-four hundred miles free. Now if the railway company is carrying rice for a distributor in Montreal twenty-four hundred miles for nothing it means that our potatoes, our cattle, our grain, and everything else must pay more in order to make up for that loss. That is really one of the problems we are facing to-day, and action is required along that line.

The Railway Commission has a great deal of responsibility, and I am not one of those who would try to increase their difficulties in any way, but I think some of these things should be looked into very carefully. As far as the East and West are concerned we know that the western rates are higher. The Railway Commission admits they are higher, and justifies the increased rate on account of the water competition in the East. That is one of the things that we hope one day will be wiped out. But I think these other discriminations in giving favoured rates to certain industries is one of the first things we should look into.

gentlemen are expecting the government to control prices they are expecting the impossible. I do not think that even my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) expects that. The question of supply has a certain bearing on prices,

1 think he will admit. As I pointed out a moment ago to the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), the department is not endeavouring to provide a supply; it simply undertakes to investigate possible sources of supply in the treatment of fuels. An investigation has been carried on having in mind the conditions to be met, because they are most acute. It does seem probable that the supply of anthracite coal will in the future be cut off from Canada, although this is not an immediate possibility. But there is a very considerable supply of bituminous coal to be had from Nova Scotia, and its treatment ought to be encouraged so that the coke may be utilized for domestic and commercial purposes in the province of Quebec. There has been a considerable agitation for the bringing of fuel from Alberta. After a
Supply-Mines

fairly thorough investigation I may say, Mr. Chairman, that that has resolved itself into a question of transportation. If rates can be cut down to the point where the fuel can be delivered in eastern Canada at a reasonable price to meet competition from the other side of the line, it has been established beyond doubt that Alberta coal will meet all demands that may be made upon it. In the meantime the work of the Dominion Fuel Board will be in the direction of research. The work planned includes:

column2: Investigation of the coking of coal for domestic use. Several plants have been erected in the United States for the purpose of coking bituminous coals in by-product recovery coke ovens with a main objective of manufacturing a domestic fuel and a gas suitable for domestic purposes.. Valuable byproducts other than gas are recovered in the coking of bituminous coal according to this process namely, ammonia or ammonium sulphate and tar oils. By-product oven coke has met with such success in those cities where householders have been instructed how to burn it, that the Fuel Board considers that this class of fuel may be introduced into Ontario and Quebec as a substitute for anthracite coal (Pennsylvania).
Central heating plants.

column1: The Dominion Fuel Board is concerned not only with the finding of a substitute for anthracite coal but with such economies as can be effected in the use of coals for heating purposes. It appears to the board that the introduction of central heating plants in highly populated centres will result in considerable economies in the use of fuel through the use of lower grade, and hence cheaper, fuel, and through the elimination of the cost3 entailed in delivering coal to private dwellings and the removal of the ashes from these dwellings. In a central heating plant, the delivery of coal may be made at one point, and all the ashes will be removed from this point. Certain municipalities in the United States and in Europe are heated by central heating plants.

column2: The adaptation of present domestic heaters to other fuels.

column1: In order to solve satisfactorily the problem of the fuel supply of the acute fuel area (the provinces of Ontario and Quebec) it is necessary that householders be assured not only of the required supply of coal, but that they may obtain this coal at the lowest possible cost. It is necessary that an investigation be undertaken with the objective of determining what alterations should or can be made in existing heaters to adapt them for burning bituminous and other coals.
Those are the three principal matters to be investigated. Then the programme provides for an investigation pertaining to the use of pulverized fuel and proceeds:

column2: The burning of pulverized fuels for generating steam for power, heating and other purposes has met with such signal success both in the United States and in Europe that it is necessary that an investigation be undertaken to ascertain whether Canadian fuels can be advantageously used in the pulverized form. The burning of fuels in the pulverized form permits of the use of the lower grade, hence cheaper, coals, and it is probable that an investigation may reveal that the low grade western lignites may be successfully used, for various purposes when pulverized, without heat or other treatment.

column1: Then, the question of freight rates is discussed, but this I will not take up the time of the committee to read. I have already discussed the question briefly. The programme continues:

column2: An investigation on the limitation in Nova Scotia coal resources and the maximum possible annual output.

column1: The possibility of introducing Nova Scotia coals into the provinces of Quebec and Ontario to reduce the imports of domestic and industrial coals from the United States is of such great importance to the solution of the fuel problem existing in the acute fuel area, that it is essential that a detailed investigation be undertaken to determine the available coal resources of Nova Scotia and the maximum possible annual output which can be economically maintained in order that the extent to which Nova Scotia coals can be depended upon to help out the fuel supply of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario may be known.

column2: An investigation of the possibility of securing and using Welsh anthracite for portions of eastern Canada.

column1: Welsh anthracite has been prominently mentioned as a substitute for a portion of the anthracite annually imported into the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. In order to determine to what extent Welsh coal can be depended upon for this purpose it is necessary to investigate the conditions governing the mining of Welsh anthracite, the freight rates from the Welsh coal mines to Canadian ports and the cost of distributing from ports to places of consumption. This investigation will also inquire into the preparation which the Welsh coals should undergo in order to suit them to Canadian conditions, also the probable markets throughout the provinces of Quebec and Ontario for this fuel.

column2: Continuation of the investigation of the possibility of utilizing peat as a partial substitute for coal.

666342,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.26,1923-05-28,06cf61a5-7c95-4155-ab94-d0d4156924b9,ca.m.931,Mr. MACLEAN (York):,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,I would suggest to the minister that the practical solution of this fuel problem is by the application of the principle of public ownership, but it must be applied in a big way, just as the power problem was solved in Ontario. For ten or fifteen years now a system has been perfected of erecting batteries of coking ovens in large centres of population and treating coal in such a way that not only the gas but certain valuable by-products are produced. The city of Toronto ought to give leadership in this respect, either in conjunction with the Consumers' Gas Company or by buying out that company and establishing a big coking plant. It has been proved beyond doubt that the most economical and effective method of heating cities like Montreal and Toronto is by means of these big coking plants. The real solution of cheap heating in our larger cities is for the government to give some kind of leadership, or, failing the federal government, for the government of Ontario or the municipal authorities of Toronto to approach this question right here and now and see what can be done. When I went along the Toronto esplanade last week the outstanding feature along that four miles of waterfront was a continuous line of great steel cars carrying from fifty to seventy tons of anthracite coal. This coal was being put into sacks, transferred

to big motor trucks and delivered to private houses. I imagine people are paying anything from $15 to $20 a ton for this anthracite, but everybody who has money is getting it, for he fears the government will do nothing, and no one wants to go through the experience endured last winter. I regret to say that the minister in bringing forward his estimates has only promises to make that further investigations will be conducted into the fuel problem. I approve of all he is doing, but he is not doing it quick enough or in a large enough way. Somebody outside ought to get busy. The province of Ontario ought to have another Beck to deal with the coal problem as the power problem was dealt with and solved years ago, that is, by co-operation and the elimination of shareholders' profits, the sole aim of the enterprise being public service. In England many large cities are being heated by central plants where the coal is coked and many valuable by-products are recovered. What can be done in the way of a solution? Investigations and reports are all right in their way, but we want action. How are the people of the cities of Canada to secure a supply of coal for the coming winter at a reasonable price and so avoid the experience of former years, but especially of last year? If the minister has some plan of that kind let him give it to us, so that progress will be made in the direction of relief.

,Independent Conservative,,William Findlay Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=06cf61a5-7c95-4155-ab94-d0d4156924b9&Language=E&Section=ALL
666343,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.27,1923-05-28,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,I do not desire to oppose this vote. I have no doubt the increase is necessary. The people are not worrying about the tesources of this country; the resources are there, in any event. The Department of Mines has done very good work in this connection, and the money has been well expended. But what the people of Canada are worrying about is where the next winter's supply of coal is to come from. There has been a great deal of discussion on this subject in both Houses of parliament; two committees have met and considered it, but we seem to be going round in a circle; we are just where we were twelve months ago. It is not a matter of research at all; the deposits are there; the question is how to get the coal out; it is a transportation question solely. I am sorry that the Railway Commission has not stepped in and taken hold of the matter. 666345,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.29,1923-05-28,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,I am not criticizing the committee; they have done a lot of good work and have procured a great deal of valuable information. I appreciate the fact that the government has done a great deal to try and reach a solution of the problem. That cannot be done in twenty-four hours, in six months or a year; it is a matter to be worked out in the days that are to come. But the average man is much disappointed, in view of the vast expenditure on the railways and canals of this country, in the failure to arrive at an arrangement which would enable these resources of western Canada and of the Maritime provinces to be brought to Ontario and Quebec. Where is the Railway Commission ' in this connection? They have not laid down a tariff for the carrying of coal to central Canada from east and west, although the commission was set up for the very purpose of regulating and fixing prices for transportation, especially of our basic products. I am sorry to see our merchant marine being sold, because I believe some of the smaller ships could bring coal from the Maritime provinces right up to the central provinces. In the early days the Canadian Pacific Railway had to carry many basic products at a loss; they did so with recurring deficits, and they struggled in those years until they made the business pay and had a surplus. I suggest that if nothing else can be done some bonus system should be worked out. The bonus system is not new in Canada; the railways were largely subsidized by bonuses. The railways to-day are carrying certain basic products to the head of the lakes at a cut rate and in my opinion they should do so with coal. Something should be done to get the coal out, because according to the coal commissioners of the province the same condition will exist next year and we will be as we were last year-people struggling round the coal offices trying to get half a ton of coal. If we bonused the transportation of this product for one winter or two or three winters we might find it to be best in the long run. The other day the Dominion Coal Company in Nova Scotia sent 30,000 tons of

coal over to Holland; that coal was badly needed in central Canada. Let the coal be carried at $5 or $6 a ton and if necessary put an amount in the estimates to cover the difference. Let us have a fair trial of this thing; if there is a deficit one year I venture to say that in two or three years there would be a surplus in the transportation of that basic product, and we would be giving employment to our own workmen and doing something to solve the transportation problem. The government, the Railway Commission-all these different bodies should get together and see whether a price cannot be fixed, even if only as an emergency measure. The Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States had to take action along similar lines. The privately-owned railways over these were quoting prohibitive prices for the transport of coal, and people in places like Cincinnati, Pittsburgh, Cleveland, Erie, Pennsylvania, places quite near the coal mines, were paying high rates of transportation. The Interstate Commerce Commission had the various bodies before them and they fixed a rate. That is what the Railway Commission here should do. Formerly 55 per cent of the coal shipments were earned by boat to lake Erie and lake Ontario ports; to-day not three per cent of it is conveyed by water-and why? I do not say there is an arrangement in restraint of trade, but there is a business arrangement under which the rates are fixed and it is decided how the coal shall be carried from the mines in Pennsylvania and elsewhere to lake Erie and lake Ontario ports and solely by rail. It is arranged that all the coal must go through the Niagara district by train to the cities, towns and villages of western Ontario. I say there is no product that is more deserving of bonus than coal is, because it is an actual necessity the same as food. This is the most important problem that the people of Canada have before them at the present time, and I hope that the government will find it possible to take some action in the matter that will afford the necessary relief.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Langton Church,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac&Language=E&Section=ALL
666346,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.30,1923-05-28,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,It is very gratifying indeed to note that our friends from Toronto are beginning to realize what it means to pay the high freight rates from Alberta down to Ontario. I would remind them that some of us up there have been paying those rates for nearly forty years. Nobody ever suggested that we should get a bonus. As a matter of fact, last year when we were wanting to get what was coming to us under the Crowsnest pass agreement and seeking to have it restored, our friends from Toronto though that a heinous proposition. Coal for the province of Ontario
Supply-Mines

is dependent upon what the people there are prepared to pay for Alberta coal. If they are prepared to pay the freight rate, plus the cost of mining, there is an abundance of coal there for all kinds of time. Our friends are suggesting a freight rate, and I understand the railways have offered a minimum freight rate, the lowest rate they can make without losing money. There is no need of anybody freezing to death next winter if they are prepared to buy this coal from Alberta or any other part of the West, and there is all kinds of it. Do they expect the government to fill all their cellars with coal? For ten years I had in a small way the supervision of the forwarding of coal during the congestion periods in Saskatchewan when the grain rush was on, and I know something of the difficulties associated with the movement of coal by railways during the grain congestion period. There is a certain amount of assistance a government can give in the way of investigational work, but to undertake to supply the domestic requirements of coal for a people, when all they have to do is to make provision for themselves, that is out of the question. There is1 coal and an abundance of it if they are prepared to pay the price. So far as a bonus is concerned, if our friends down here require a bonus to haul their coal from Alberta, I do not know that I will object to it so much; I sympathize with them on this long haul, but when discussing freight rates again, and the whole Crowsnest agreement is not restored yet-we are paying for these long hauls and have been doing it for forty years, some of us-I would like to see the sympathy reciprocated a little more in the future than it has been in the past.

666352,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.36,1923-05-28,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil):,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,As I tried to point out in the beginning of the discussion,
Supply-Mines

we do not consider it our duty to provide the supply. What we are endeavouring to do is to investigate the possibilities of using the lower grade bituminous coals that can be procured from Canada and the United States and treating them so that they will take the place of anthracite. Then there is the other vital question, that of freight rates. So far as the Alberta product is concerned that does not need investigation so far as the Mines department is concerned. It is a question of transportation pure and simple. There is no treatment of the Alberta product required. That has been demonstrated both in Toronto and this city so that the problem of using Alberta coal is simply one of transportation, and if the rate oan be reduced to a level that will make it possible to bring that coal down here, that problem will be solved.

There seems to be on the part of the committee an intimation that the government should do something to secure a supply of coal. We have a committee, headed by Mr. Magrath, which has been working more or less on the question of distribution. We have not interfered in that field at all, but there is a bituminous field in the United States close to the city of Toronto that we are investigating. Perhaps that coal could be used in central heating plants or be coked, using the by-products, turning the gas, for instance, into the gas mains and utilizing it for heat and light if necessary. The other by-products would also find a ready market in Toronto. I am told that that coal can be delivered in Toronto for around 87 a ton to-day even at the high rates of transportation prevailing, and that it could be made into a product that could be sold reasonably at ten or eleven dollars a ton, and that it would be equal to anthracite. That is a problem of investigation that we are now working on. If the municipality of Toronto or the provincial government desires to undertake distribution or even to set up a coking plant, there is nothing in the world to prevent them.
