column2: Canada possesses large undeveloped water powers and these have come to be considered by many people as a possible source of electric energy that might be used for heating houses and buildings. It is important that the physical and economic limitations of the use of electric energy for house heating purposes should be thoroughly investigated. The Dominion Fuel Board includes as one of its members the Director of the Water Powers branch, Department of the Interior, and can appropriately undertake a study of the subject.

column1: And then there is (10) the question of house construction in order that better insulation be developed. That, of course, does not apply to buildings already constructed. That is the programme that the fuel committee have laid out for investigation and for which we are asking the sum of $53,000.

666361,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.45,1923-05-28,78eadf97-c6a9-462a-b669-6f6616adf0ba,ca.m.7702,Mr. CARROLL:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,I do not think it hurts the various departments of the government to be criticized occasionally by the very faithful followers of the administration. Objection may not, perhaps, be raised to the passage of
Supply-Mines

this vote for ascertaining whether or not we may be able to treat American bituminous coal in the various cities of Ontario in order to get a supply of fuel from this source. I should rather think, however, that the Mines department of this country should exercise its intellect, and employ its knowledge in showing parliament and the country whether or not it is possible to bring the bituminous coal of eastern Canada and the bituminous coal of western Canada into the central cities of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, there to be manufactured into coke and so take the place of the anthracite which we have been importing from the United States.

,Liberal,,William F. Carroll,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=78eadf97-c6a9-462a-b669-6f6616adf0ba&Language=E&Section=ALL
666362,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.46,1923-05-28,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil):,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,May I interrupt the hon. gentleman to say that is exactly what we propose to do. The same treatment will be applied to the bituminous coal of the Maritime provinces as to the bituminous coal of the West. Let me say to my hon. friend that I have no desire to encourage the use of United States fuel at the expense of the Canadian fuel.

,Liberal,,Charles A. Stewart,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b&Language=E&Section=ALL
666363,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.47,1923-05-28,78eadf97-c6a9-462a-b669-6f6616adf0ba,ca.m.7702,Mr. CARROLL:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,Then I misunderstood

the minister. I should rather think the first thing this government, or any Canadian government, would do would be to investigate the possibilities of a Canadian supply. If, as the result of future investigations, they find that they are unable to obtain a supply of fuel in this country, then they might turn their thoughts to the United States. When I spoke as I did a few minutes ago of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) who has been a live wire in our committee and who has taken more interest in the committee on Mines and Minerals-which is now holding sittings for the first time I think in twenty years-than any other member I can now point my finger at, I thought perhaps we had better leave the discussion of this question until the report of that committee was brought down. However, the minister has brought in an estimate with respect to fuel which affords us an opportunity of discussing this question. I still think I must have misunderstood the minister, or he did not make the matter quite plain to me. In his answer to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) I understood him to say that this $53,000 was for the purpose of treating United States coal in order to obtain a supply of fuel for Canada. Now, this whole matter has been fully investigated by both the Senate committee and the House of Commons committee. I am not suggesting that the minister hold this vote over, but I would ask him to consider very

seriously the spending of any money in an investigation looking to the United States for a supply of coal. The very purpose of the inquiry of both committees has been, as I understand it, to ascertain whether or not Canada is to-day in a position to supply the fuel demands of this country. I for one would rather object to spending our money for any other purpose than to ascertain whether we may entertain the hope in the near future of being able to supply the national demands from domestic sources. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this is a most serious question. I agree with my hon. friend, the member for North Toronto, that it is the most serious question that has arisen in Canada for some time. If we had a thousand war ships on the Great Lakes in the event of a war with the United States-which God forbid may ever become a fact-that would avail us nothing under present conditions in Canada, because the United States could cut off our fuel supply in twenty-four hours. In that short period of time we would have to capitulate to every demand that might be made upon us to the great republic to the south. Therefore in that respect the fuel question is of national importance and demands the serious consideration of parliament and the country.

The Minister of Agriculture said a moment ago that we have been labouring under the difficulty of freight rates for years. I would like to show him a few telegrams which were sent a few days ago to our committee by the coal operators of the West. Perhaps the minister has seen those telegrams. When Sir Henry Thornton made his railway rate of $9 a ton for the transportation of fuel from the coal fields of Alberta to the various centres in the East, he suggested that the coal operators, and others interested, might join in cutting down their profits.

,Liberal,,William F. Carroll,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=78eadf97-c6a9-462a-b669-6f6616adf0ba&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,William Richard Motherwell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f&Language=E&Section=ALL
666365,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.49,1923-05-28,78eadf97-c6a9-462a-b669-6f6616adf0ba,ca.m.7702,Mr. CARROLL:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,I want to tell the Minister of Agriculture that we got very little encouragement from the coal operators of the West in that respect. They simply said that it was impossible for them to get coal into Ontario at a freight rate of $9 a ton, but they made no comment as to whether or not they would contribute in reducing the cost in order that coal might be brought to the people who needed it. That is one of the things, I think, Sir Henry Thornton intended to bring very forcibly to the coal operators of this country. Therefore, when you talk
Supply-Mines

about freight and lake rates, and similar charges, do not lay the whole blame for existing conditions on the railroads of Canada. If this is becoming a national question, as it undoubtedly is, I think a conference should be held in the immediate future between representatives of the Dominion government. and the various local governments so that the whole matter may be gone into in a very searching manner. No company in this country owns the coal deposits. In the prairie provinces I presume they are owned by the Dominion government. In the Maritime and older provinces they are owned by the local governments, and while I do not wish to make any accusations against operators or persons who are carrying coal, I would say the time has come, Mr. Chairman, when the cards of the various provinces should be laid on the table, and when there should be an open conference with the coal operators of the country, and they should be brought to a realization of the fact that the coal industry of Canada is a national asset, not owned by any company, not owned by any man, but owned by the people at large. I am in hopes that will be one of the things our committee will recommend to the members of this House. I do not wish to criticize the item, but I say, in view of the treatment which has been accorded to Canada, in the last year, that I, as a humble member and faithful follower of this government, would suggest that they should go slowly in spending any part of this $53,000 towards advertising American wares in the shape of coal shipped into this country. Perhaps I misunderstood the minister. I know he is just as true a Canadian as I am, and perhaps better, but, in view of all the circumstances, I would think the energies of his department should be directed more closely towards a very sincere investigation of the possibilities of a home supply for Canada than the probabilities of our demand being satisfied from a foreign country.

,Liberal,,William F. Carroll,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=78eadf97-c6a9-462a-b669-6f6616adf0ba&Language=E&Section=ALL
666366,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.50,1923-05-28,a1744cb8-5f98-47d2-80e0-a977df75578a,ca.m.8322,Mr. MILLAR:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,I wish to press a certain matter on the minister briefly. I had a conversation with a mining engineer a week ago, and I had intended to get my information in better shape before the item came up; still I think I can give him the kernel of the conversation. This conversation showed the necessity of getting accurate reports in regard to our natural resources. This gentleman did not mention this matter by way of criticism of the department, and yet the conversation developed a weak spot. He stated that on one occasion the engineer representing the department brought in some samples from mines located away out in the extreme north that tested out very good indeed. He and some friends had some interests near at hand, and sent out representatives to get samples of ore, and found the samples tested very poorly. They wondered that there was such a discrepancy and where the fault lay. They sent out a second group of prospectors, with the same result. His explanation was that the samples that had been taken by the representative of the department had been salted, if hon. members are familiar with that term, and he remarked that if one were going to be entirely accurate it was necessary almost to lock up his samples after he had taken them, lest some sharper might drop something into them in order to give an entirely false report. He and his friends had been put to the expense of some thousands of dollars just because the report was not accurate. This shows the necessity of obtaining accurate information.

In regard to coal, it strikes me it would be most difficult-and I would be glad to think it would be possible-to bring Alberta coal to Ontario and sell it for ten or eleven dollars per ton. Some hon. members do not seem to wish to continue this

11 p.m. discussion, but I have not taken very much time and I did not introduce it. The question has been introduced and discussed at considerable length. Some people have thought that the coal we ha're been discussing is not going to give satisfaction, and that it will slack. I have used this coal entirely for two years. I have found no difficulty with the coal slacking. Sometimes I have had tons left over in the spring of the year, and have used them in the fall and found no difficulty from slacking. It is simply a question of freight rates, as to whether it is going to be possible to bring coal from Alberta to Toronto and sell it for $9 or $10 a ton. I and others in my town paid last winter $13 a ton on the car. Either it is a case of paying very exorbitant freight rates, or else it will be impossible to bring it to Ontario and sell it in Toronto for $10 or $11 a ton. I would be glad to think it rould be done, and that we could save the $60,000,000 that goes to the United States annually for coal. I can see one of our difficulties that has not yet been touched on in the debate. Perhaps some hon. gentlemen who have a lot of labour people in their constituencies are a little reluctant about touching on it. One of the great difficulties is the problem presented by labour. I believe a great many in the ranks of labour are not
Supply-Mines

receiving too much. A great many who are serving on railways are not receiving too much, but I am convinced there are a goodly number receiving far too much. Here is the way it works out. I had a talk with a friend last fall who stated he had stayed over in the north country with a repairer of engines who, in the course of conversation had said, ""I have been able to count 25 hours a day for the last three months"". ""Well"" my friend ""when do you sleep?"" ""Oh"" he said, ""you doubt it. I will show you by my book. If I work half an hour I am paid for half a day, and if I work after hours I am paid time and a half."" And he went on to say further that the engineer helped him out some. He said, ""If an engineer comes in at five in the afternoon the engine is not reported till after six. In that way I get paid time and a half for repairing, but if an engine arrives in the morning, say at five o'clock, that engine is reported at once. It may be too warm so that I cannot repair it at once, but it is reported, and being reported at once I get paid time and a half fob repairing it."" You may say this is just hearsay but it did not pass through very many mouths- just one-before it reached me. From other sources, from men in the offices, I have gathered the same information. In that way some men are able to draw far more pay than they have a right to.

666370,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.54,1923-05-28,a1744cb8-5f98-47d2-80e0-a977df75578a,ca.m.8322,Mr. MILLAR:,,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,A conference was mentioned a few moments ago by the member who has asked me the question. It seems to me something might be done by a conference between labour, capital and representatives of the government. In many cases unemployed workmen are not only anxious but willing to work for a fair wage but they are unable to secure employment because others in the ranks of labour are demanding more than they are entitled to, and are thereby stiffing industry. There would be a great deal more employment if these high wages were not demanded. The railways would be able to carry freight for much less and that would give an impetus to mining and make it possible to bring coal from Alberta to Ontario and sell it at a reasonable ' price. That is one way in which a conference could accomplish a great deal of good. I do not wish to prolong the discussion, but I [Mr. Millar. J

would offer the same suggestion put forward by an hon. gentleman from Toronto; I should be sorry to see the ships belonging to the Merchant Marine sold. I think they should be kept, in view of the combine which we have seen on the lakes. I think it might be well to keep them in use.

These three new positions are to be filled by officers who will be in the Fuel Testing division, engaged in the very work we have been discussing; that is to say, an engineer grade No. 3, at $2,700, an assistant chemist at $2,100, and a junior chemist at $1,680, making a total of . $6,480. Reclassification accounts for $3,792.50. These, together with the statutory increases of $14,755, make up the total increase of $25,027.50.

,Liberal,,Charles A. Stewart,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b&Language=E&Section=ALL
666380,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.64,1923-05-28,d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2,ca.m.4870,Mr. MEIGHEN:,Leader of the Official Opposition,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,You can always make up an increase if you employ a sufficient number of new men and do not get any extra services from the men you already have, while their salaries are moving up. The increase of salaries implies that extra services are being obtained for it. Every few days we get an advertisement from the Civil Service Commission wanting to appoint this, that, and the other man at large or comparatively large salaries, for some new positions that are created. If this goes on, where are we going to land? If we look for reductions we find them only in connection with help given by the Dominion to provinces or municipalities, thereby saving the taxpayers' money paid to those authorities. The increases come in the civil government estimates in the various departments one after the other; they are going on apparently recklessly. This relatively is an enormous in-

crease-$25,000. At this rate of increase per year the department is going to reach the dimensions of the Interior department. Why all these ""chemists? I was only in charge of the Mines department a very short time, and the department ended with fewer chemists while I was there.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Arthur Meighen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2&Language=E&Section=ALL
666381,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.65,1923-05-28,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil):,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,I am advised that during the period of the war the department was almost denuded of chemists, they being attracted from the service by various commercial enterprises. The same applies to the engineers in this particular department. If there is an excuse for an expenditure in any department of government, I do think it is in the Mines department in which an attempt is made to ascertain the amount of our natural resources and their utilization, and of course chemists play a very important part in any development of this character. The three additional chemists that I am asking for this year will be utilized, as I pointed out a few minutes ago, in carrying on the fuel investigation.

,Liberal,,Charles A. Stewart,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b&Language=E&Section=ALL
666382,ca.proc.d.1923-05-28.48.10.66,1923-05-28,d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2,ca.m.4870,Mr. MEIGHEN:,Leader of the Official Opposition,SUPPLY-U.S. LABOUR DELEGATES DETAINED CASE OE ALEXANDER HOWAT,MINES DEPARTMENT,,There was some reduction all right, and there was a very considerable censure upon us for not reducing the staff still more; but the process is now in operation. It is true we need chemists, but I do think if you have a limited number of good, faithful men, and they are made to understand that they must concentrate their work upon purely practical ends, we will get as good results at far less eost to the countiy. The temptation of the permanent heads to enlarge the operations under them is very great, and the pressure from those heads is always upon the minister to accede to their demands, but I would warn the minister not to be too easily impressed even by the best of deputies-and I think he has one of the best in that department.
